articles.title: Condephaat pede ampliação de espaço entre gradil e CCC de Campinas | G1
articles.standfirst: Embora mantenha previsão de cercamento, conselho quer áreas mais amplas entre o gradil e os acessos ao Teatro de Arena; prazo de análise pode chegar a 180 dias.
articles.summary: Embora mantenha previsão de cercamento, conselho quer áreas mais amplas entre o gradil e os acessos ao Teatro de Arena; prazo de análise pode chegar a 180 dias.
articles.body:
Gradis de aço instalados no entorno do Centro de Convivência Cultura de Campinas (SP): Prefeitura diz que espaço permanecerá aberto à população ads 8h às 19h — Foto: Daniel Ribeiro

O projeto de cercamento do Centro de Convivência Cultural de Campinas passará por nova análise do Conselho de Defesa do Patrimônio Histórico, Arqueológico, Artístico e Turístico (Condephaat) após a prefeitura apresentar nova proposta. Embora o gradil permaneça previsto , o órgão estadual orientou alterações para ampliar a distância entre as cercas e as escadarias de acesso ao Teatro de Arena .

Segundo o Condephaat, a recomendação é que o município considere aspectos relacionados à circulação de pessoas e ao paisagismo do espaço .

"O Condephaat informa que orientou a Prefeitura de Campinas a considerar questões de fluidez na circulação e de paisagismo, além de uma nova alternativa para o gradil de cercamento ao redor do Centro de Convivência Cultural, no sentido de ampliar os espaços entre as escadas de acesso ao Teatro de Arena e o gradil, para transformá-los em largos mais generosos", informou o órgão.

✅ Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 Campinas no WhatsApp

Em nota, a Secretaria Municipal de Cultural reformou que o cercamento permanece previsto no projeto e é necessário para garantir a segurança e a preservação das estruturas implantadas durante a reforma, especialmente do sistema de impermeabilização.

"Considerado um dos pontos mais sensíveis da obra, esse sistema exige técnica especializada e alto investimento e pode ser comprometido por ações como furos, fogo ou qualquer rompimento da camada impermeável, o que pode provocar infiltrações e prejuízos significativos. Além disso, o cercamento permite maior controle e proteção da área durante o período de garantia técnica da obra", diz a nota.

A instalação do gradil foi concluída pela prefeitura em julho de 2025 , e o cercamento da estrutura reaberta depois de 14 anos gerou debate nas redes sociais e foi definido como "um retrocesso urbanístico" pela Associação Brasileira dos Escritórios de Arquitetura (Asbea-SP).

O cercamento do Centro de Convivência é alvo de questionamentos na Justiça por meio de uma ação popular acompanhada pelo Ministério Público de São Paulo (MP-SP).

Em junho, o promotor Paulo César Martinez manifestou-se pela suspensão do prazo processual por 60 dias para que a prefeitura possa informar o andamento das tratativas com o Condephaat.

A nova proposta foi protocolada no fim de julho e segue em análise pelo órgão estadual. Em nota, o Condephaat informou que o prazo total para análise do protocolo até uma eventual aprovação é de até 180 dias .

➡️ Apesar do cercamento, a Secretaria de Cultura destaca que o Teatro de Arena do Centro de Convivência abre ao público diariamente, das 7h às 21h.

Em comunicado enviado ao g1 , a Associação Brasileira dos Escritórios de Arquitetura (Asbea-SP) manifestou contrariedade a decisão do Condepacc , e definiu que a medida representa "um grave retrocesso do ponto de vista urbanístico e um atentado ao direito à cidade."

"O Centro de Convivência foi concebido pelo arquiteto Fábio Penteado como um espaço aberto, democrático e acessível, voltado à convivência, ao encontro e à expressão cultural. Cercá-lo contraria frontalmente sua vocação original e compromete sua função como equipamento público integrador", afirma a associação.

Ainda segundo a Asbea-SP, que pede que a prefeitura e o Condepacc reavaliem a decisão, o fechamento de espaço público com gradis, sob a ótica do urbanismo, acarreta uma série de impactos negativos. São eles:

Rompe com a continuidade e fluidez do tecido urbano, isolando áreas que deveriam ser permeáveis e integradas à vida cotidiana da cidade;

Enfraquece a segurança no longo prazo, ao reduzir a presença ativa de pessoas, favorecendo o esvaziamento e a degradação do espaço;

Desvaloriza o espaço público como lugar de convivência e bem coletivo, substituindo a ideia de cidadania pela lógica do controle e da exclusão.

"É essencial buscar soluções mais sensatas, sustentáveis e coerentes com os princípios de uma cidade inclusiva, acessível e viva", destaca a Asbea.

Campinas entregou teatro do Centro de Convivência de Campinas — Foto: Firmino Piton/Prefeitura de Campinas

Campinas entregou, no dia 10 de julho de 2025, a obra do Centro de Convivência, fechado desde 2011. A conclusão encerrou um impasse de 14 anos em que um dos maiores equipamentos culturais da metrópole ficou sem uso.

A reforma do Convivência passou por uma série de problemas, contestações, suspensões de licitações e atrasos ao longo dos anos.

A obra foi dividida em duas fases - que também tiveram prorrogações de prazo. O valor total foi de R$ 62,4 milhões.

articles.title: Premiê de Israel chama governantes do Irã de 'selvagens' | G1
articles.standfirst: Benjamin Netanyahu disse em evento que não acredita em uma saída diplomática pra guerra e contou que falou isso para o presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump.
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu disse em evento que não acredita em uma saída diplomática pra guerra e contou que falou isso para o presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump.
articles.body:
O primeiro-ministro israelense, Benjamin Netanyahu — Foto: REUTERS/Ronen Zvulun/Pool

O primeiro-ministro de Israel , Benjamin Netanyahu , chamou os governantes do Irã de "selvagens" e afirmou não acreditar que uma saída diplomática é possível para encerrar a guerra.

✅ Siga o canal de notícias internacionais do g1 no WhatsApp

Em um evento na noite desta terça-feira (25), Netanyahu contou que falou isso ao presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , em um encontro recente. Ele também elogiou a campanha de pressão econômica promovida pelo aliado contra Teerã.

"Duvido que seja possível chegar a um acordo com aquele grupo lá, com aqueles selvagens. Eu digo a vocês: um acordo não pode ser alcançado", declarou.

Um dia antes, o primeiro-ministro israelense havia acusado o Irã de tentar assassinar um dos filhos dele , mas não especificou qual deles, nem quando ou onde teria ocorrido a tentativa.

O primeiro-ministro israelense tem dois filhos e uma filha.

“Aconteceu algo inacreditável: o Irã mirou em um dos meus filhos. O Irã tentou matar um dos meus filhos”, declarou Netanyahu durante uma entrevista por telefone ao canal Channel 14.

articles.title: Poste desaba e fere mulher e criança em Copacabana, na Zona Sul do Rio | G1
articles.standfirst: Estrutura caiu sobre as vítimas na Avenida Nossa Senhora de Copacabana. As duas foram levadas ao Hospital Municipal Miguel Couto e não correm risco de vida.
articles.summary: Após o poste cair em Copacabana, as vítimas foram levadas ao Hospital Miguel Couto com ferimentos, mas estão fora de perigo segundo a Secretaria de Saúde.
articles.body:
Um poste desabou sobre uma mulher e uma criança na noite de terça-feira (25), em Copacabana, na Zona Sul do Rio. As vítimas foram socorridas e levadas para o Hospital Municipal Miguel Couto.

O acidente aconteceu na Avenida Nossa Senhora de Copacabana, na altura da Rua Dias da Rocha, e foi registrado por câmeras de segurança da região. Após a queda da estrutura metálica, a área foi interditada.

📱Baixe o app do g1 para ver notícias do RJ em tempo real e de graça

Poste metálico caiu sobre criança e mulher em Copacabana — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

Segundo testemunhas, a mulher, de cerca de 35 anos, e a criança, de 5, caminhavam de mãos dadas quando foram atingidas. O local fica próximo a um ponto de ônibus de grande movimento.

“Eu estava no meu local de trabalho, tinha acabado de chegar e só escutei um barulho. Muita gente começou a correr. Nesse momento, vi a estrutura no chão, e a moça e a criança estavam feridas”, contou Adilson Miranda, porteiro de um prédio em frente ao local do acidente.

Moradores e pedestres prestaram os primeiros socorros até a chegada dos bombeiros, que atenderam as vítimas em menos de 15 minutos. O atendimento inicial foi feito na calçada antes da remoção para o hospital.

articles.standfirst: Evento deve passar por dez cidades localizadas no Brejo da Paraíba entre os meses de julho a setembro.
articles.summary: O evento Caminhos do Frio 2026 inicia programação em Alagoa Grande com shows, oficinas e gastronomia, percorrendo dez cidades do Brejo paraibano até setembro.
articles.body:
Geraldo Azevedo é uma das atrações confirmadas no Caminhos do Frio — Foto: Divulgação

A Rota Cultural Caminhos do Frio 2026 chega a cidade de Alagoa Grande nesta quarta-feira (26). O circuito vai passar por vários municípios do Brejo paraibano até o mês de setembro, e em Alagoa Grande nomes como Geraldo Azevedo estão confirmados em shows na cidade.

A Rota Cultural Caminhos do Frio completa 20 anos em 2026 e conta com uma programação cultural que oferece aos visitantes música, artes cênicas, gastronomia, trilhas e experiências nos engenhos.

✅ Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 PB no WhatsApp

Em Alagoa Grande a programação segue até 30 de agosto com shows, oficinas, trilhas, atividades literárias e exposições. Geraldo Azevedo se apresenta no palco principal da festa, em praça pública, no sábado (29).

A programação completa do Caminhos do Frio em Alagoa Grande pode ser conferida nas redes sociais da prefeitura da cidade. Fazem parte da rota cultural as cidades de Areia, Pilões, Matinhas, Solânea, Serraria, Borborema, Remígio, Bananeiras, Alagoa Grande e Alagoa Nova ( confira o cronograma das cidades ).

articles.title: Quem era o adolescente que morreu afogado em praia de Palmas | G1
articles.standfirst: Daniel Brand Peres Rodrigues, de 15 anos, foi descrito por familiares e amigos como um jovem trabalhador, sonhador e apaixonado por futebol. A morte do adolescente, após se afogar na Praia do Caju, em Palmas.
articles.summary: Daniel Brand Peres Rodrigues, de 15 anos, foi descrito por familiares e amigos como um jovem trabalhador, sonhador e apaixonado por futebol. A morte do adolescente, após se afogar.
articles.body:
Trabalhador, dedicado aos estudos, apegado à família e apaixonado por futebol. Essas são algumas das características de Daniel Brand Peres Rodrigues, de 15 anos, descritas pelo amigo João Marcos. Daniel morreu afogado no último domingo (23), enquanto nadava na Praia do Caju , em Palmas .

"Para falar sobre esse rapaz a gente até se emociona, porque era um jovem que tinha muitos sonhos pela frente. Não dava trabalho para os pais, sempre obedecia à mãe, era cristão e com 15 anos, já tinha as suas responsabilidades. Trabalhava com o tio para ajudar a mãe e conseguir as coisinhas dele. O que tivesse de serviço em lote, de ajudante, ele estava fazendo", relatou João Marcos.

Segundo o Corpo de Bombeiros, testemunhas relataram que o jovem tentava atravessar um trecho do lago nadando quando submergiu e não voltou à superfície. Ele foi encontrado e levado até a margem, onde uma equipe do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) realizou manobras de reanimação cardiopulmonar (RCP), mas o adolescente não resistiu.

📱 Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 TO no WhatsApp

Conforme o amigo, além de ser dedicado ao trabalho, Daniel também priorizava os estudos e havia iniciado um curso de capacitação. Nas horas de lazer, a principal paixão do adolescente era o futebol. Comunicativo e querido pelos colegas, ele aproveitava os momentos livres para jogar bola.

Jovem de 15 anos trabalhava com o tio para ajudar nas despesas de casa — Foto: Reprodução/Assembleia de Deus nova geração do avivamento

Adolescente morre afogado enquanto nadava em praia de Palmas, dizem bombeiros

Filhote de cachorro é encontrado carbonizado após queimada em terreno baldio no TO

Médicos e enfermeiros são investigados pela morte de jovem no dia que seria libertado de presídio após ser absolvido

Amigo de infância de Daniel, João Marcos conta que os dois se conheceram na igreja que frequentavam com as famílias e mantinham uma relação de convivência e parceria no dia a dia. Segundo ele, Daniel era determinado e sonhava em construir o próprio futuro.

"Na última conversa que tive com ele, nós sorrimos muito e eu disse: 'Continua assim, obedecendo a sua mãe, trabalhando e correndo atrás dos seus objetivos'. Ele era um menino de ouro, com um coração muito bom.

João conta que a morte de Daniel causou grande comoção entre familiares, amigos e membros da igreja. "Quando soube da fatalidade, fiquei desesperado. É muito triste perder alguém com tanta vontade de vencer", desabafou.

Após a confirmação da morte, a escola onde ele estudava decretou luto oficial. O velório foi realizado na segunda-feira (24).

articles.title: Museu de Ciências Naturais realiza observação de eclipse lunar | G1
articles.standfirst: As atividades têm início às 18h30 e se estendem até às 3h de sexta-feira (28). Os ingressos podem ser retirados pelo site.
articles.summary: As atividades têm início às 18h30 e se estendem até às 3h de sexta-feira (28). Os ingressos podem ser retirados pelo site.
articles.body:
Observatório do Museu de Ciências Naturais PUC Minas — Foto: Divulgação

O Museu de Ciências Naturais PUC Minas realiza, nesta quinta-feira (27), uma programação especial noturna para observação do eclipse lunar com telescópios. As atividades tem início às 18h30 e se estendem até às 3h de sexta-feira (28). Os ingressos podem ser retirados pelo site ( veja mais abaixo ).

Além da observação, haverá quatro sessões do Planeário, focadas em explicar de forma didática e imersiva a mecânica celeste do eclipse. As sessões serão às 19h, 20h, 21 e 22h.

Para participar da observação, é necessário adquirir um ingresso para o Museu , que custa R$ 20, com opções de meia-entrada. Para ter a experiência completa, os interessados podem adquirir o combo Museu + Planetário, no valor de R$ 32, que também possui opções de meia-entrada.

Além do site, os ingressos podem ser retirados na bilheteria local, mas as vagas são limitadas.

articles.title: Sugar prices: Indiaâs sugar squeeze threatens its biggest season for sweets
articles.summary: Domestic sugar prices have jumped nearly 40%, forcing India to import 1 million tonnes of the sweetener.
articles.body:
India, the world's largest consumer of sugar, is trying to avoid a bittersweet festive season.

Sugar prices have jumped nearly 40% in the past two months, prompting the government to import 1 million tonnes for the first time in nearly a decade.

The move comes as demand surges from August, with festivals such as Ganesh Chaturthi, Dussehra and Diwali leading into the busy wedding season. Food and beverage companies also begin stocking up for one of their busiest sales periods, adding pressure on wholesale prices.

Production is now expected to be 30.6 million tonnes in the current season, which runs from October 2025 to September 2026 - 11% below the government's earlier estimate of 34.3 million tonnes.

The squeeze has sent prices soaring. A kilo of sugar that cost around 40-45 rupees ($0.42-0.47; Â£0.31-0.35) in May-June was selling for more than 58-60 rupees in several markets in August, although prices have begun to ease slightly.

But how did a country, which is also the world's second-largest sugar producer, end up needing imports?

The government has blamed lower sugarcane production linked to reduced rainfall during El NiÃ±o, hoarding and tighter global supplies after adverse weather hit other major producers.

But experts say another key factor was that India overestimated its own production - and allowed sugar to be exported before the extent of the shortfall became clear.

The government initially approved exports of 1.5 million tonnes this season, adding another 500,000 tonnes in February. Nearly 800,000 tonnes had been shipped before exports were halted in May.

"From allowing exports at the start of the season to ending with an import of a million tonnes is a large variation on production estimates - and that's a big surprise," said Vikram Suryavanshi, a senior analyst at PhillipCapital India.

That matters because India has little sugar to spare. It consumed more than 28 million tonnes last season, not far below what it expects to produce this year.

Nearly three million tonnes is also expected to be diverted to ethanol production, leaving little room for any shortfall.

That is where the imports will help provide a buffer, says Atul Chaturvedi, non-executive director of Shree Renuka Sugars, India's largest sugar refiner and a major ethanol producer.

For three months from 1 September, sugar refineries in special economic zones near ports - which normally import raw sugar, refine it and re-export it - will be allowed to sell duty-free sugar in the domestic market.

The last time India imported sugar for domestic consumption was nearly a decade ago, when the country was grappling with drought.

Other measures are also under way. The Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA) has asked mills to begin crushing cane a fortnight earlier than usual to build stocks as the new harvest starts arriving in October.

But that crop, too, faces risks from erratic weather.

Sugarcane is highly water-intensive, and uneven monsoon rains and prolonged dry spells in key growing states such as Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka have affected the crop. Yields are expected to fall, while thinner cane with lower sucrose content means less sugar can be produced.

"Looking at the climate conditions, the next season is also not going to be a bumper crop, although it is too early for actual assessment," Chaturvedi said.

India has frequently restricted agricultural exports when domestic supplies tighten and prices rise. In 2023, for instance, it banned exports of non-basmati white rice for more than a year after crop damage contributed to rising food prices.

But experts say the failure to anticipate the sugar shortfall before allowing exports has raised questions about the government's forecasts.

"This year, the initial projections for sugarcane production did not materialise due to unusual weather in some parts and disease in certain varieties," said Siraj Hussain, a former secretary at the federal agriculture ministry.

The government has not explained why the scale of the shortfall was not identified before exports were halted on 13 May. It has said production fell below estimates because of sugarcane disease and waterlogging caused by excessive rainfall.

The BBC has contacted the agriculture ministry for comment.

Some commentators have also blamed the diversion of sugarcane to ethanol production for the shortage in a deficit year. Even earlier, sugar mills would set aside around 10% of their output for this, helping stabilise prices in times of excess production.

But India making E20, or petrol blended with 20% ethanol, the standard fuel at pumps this year, just as sugar output is low, has added to the challenge, experts say.

The government disputes how much the policy is to blame. It says the share of cane diverted to ethanol has fallen from 12% in 2022-23 to around 9% in 2025-26, and argues that weak production, hoarding and tighter global supplies are behind the sugar price surge.

Some in the industry agree. Deepak Ballani of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA), which represents private mills producing nearly half of India's sugar, says stocks and monthly quotas for sugar released into the market are comfortable. He argues speculation and hoarding, rather than a genuine shortage, are driving prices higher.

The government has capped stocks held by traders and wholesalers at 400 tonnes for three months to curb hoarding.

Suryavanshi, however, disagrees. India has used such measures before, he says, yet prices continued to climb after the latest restrictions were announced. To him, that points to a real supply squeeze.

And India's decision to import comes as supplies are tightening globally.

El NiÃ±o has affected rainfall in Thailand, while heavy rain has disrupted cane harvesting in Brazil, the world's largest sugar producer, where mills are also diverting more cane to ethanol. Heatwaves have battered Europe's sugar beet crop, with France expecting its worst harvest in four years.

US government forecasters expect global production to fall to 184.9 million tonnes this season, from a record 186.1 million tonnes the year before.

London white sugar futures hit $541 a tonne in mid-August, their highest since April 2025, while New York raw sugar futures jumped 4% on the day India announced its imports.

For India, however, sugar availability could improve next year if high prices prompt mills to divert less cane to ethanol.

"At current sugar prices, it simply doesn't make economic sense for mills to divert cane juice to ethanol, so India's sugar scenario should be quite all right going forward," Chaturvedi said.

But the bigger lesson from this year's squeeze, he added, is clear: it is a "warning that going forward, we need to be a lot more careful in estimating our sugar crop numbers".

The government has not explained why the scale of the shortfall was not identified before exports were halted on 13 May. It has said production fell below estimates because of sugarcane disease and waterlogging caused by excessive rainfall.
The BBC has contacted the agriculture ministry for comment.

Some commentators have also blamed the diversion of sugarcane to ethanol production for the shortage in a deficit year. Even earlier, sugar mills would set aside around 10% of their output for this, helping stabilise prices in times of excess production.
But India making E20, or petrol blended with 20% ethanol, the standard fuel at pumps this year, just as sugar output is low, has added to the challenge, experts say.

The government disputes how much the policy is to blame. It says the share of cane diverted to ethanol has fallen from 12% in 2022-23 to around 9% in 2025-26, and argues that weak production, hoarding and tighter global supplies are behind the sugar price surge.

Some in the industry agree. Deepak Ballani of the Indian Sugar Mills Association (ISMA), which represents private mills producing nearly half of India's sugar, says stocks and monthly quotas for sugar released into the market are comfortable. He argues speculation and hoarding, rather than a genuine shortage, are driving prices higher.
The government has capped stocks held by traders and wholesalers at 400 tonnes for three months to curb hoarding.

Suryavanshi, however, disagrees. India has used such measures before, he says, yet prices continued to climb after the latest restrictions were announced. To him, that points to a real supply squeeze.
And India's decision to import comes as supplies are tightening globally.

El NiÃ±o has affected rainfall in Thailand, while heavy rain has disrupted cane harvesting in Brazil, the world's largest sugar producer, where mills are also diverting more cane to ethanol. Heatwaves have battered Europe's sugar beet crop, with France expecting its worst harvest in four years.
US government forecasters expect global production to fall to 184.9 million tonnes this season, from a record 186.1 million tonnes the year before.
London white sugar futures hit $541 a tonne in mid-August, their highest since April 2025, while New York raw sugar futures jumped 4% on the day India announced its imports.
For India, however, sugar availability could improve next year if high prices prompt mills to divert less cane to ethanol.
"At current sugar prices, it simply doesn't make economic sense for mills to divert cane juice to ethanol, so India's sugar scenario should be quite all right going forward," Chaturvedi said.
But the bigger lesson from this year's squeeze, he added, is clear: it is a "warning that going forward, we need to be a lot more careful in estimating our sugar crop numbers".

articles.title: South Korea police find four bodies on Jeju island as missing persons scandal deepens
articles.summary: A police sergeant has been arrested following accusations that he lied to victims' families and prematurely closed missing persons cases.
articles.body:
Four missing people have been found dead on South Korean holiday island Jeju, as local police face mounting public criticism for allegedly mishandling missing persons cases.

Reports emerged last week that authorities were launching a belated search for a woman reported missing months ago. This sparked criticism of the police for failing to search for her earlier.

The scandal has since deepened with the arrest of a police sergeant, surnamed Bu, who is accused of lying to victims' families and prematurely closing missing persons cases.

Four officers in the sergeant's chain of command have been put on administrative leave and on Tuesday President Lee Jae Myung ordered a sweeping reform of the police force.

Since Saturday, police have found four bodies on the island, including that of 37-year-old Jang Mi-ran who had gone missing in May.

On Monday, her body was located at a palm tree farm about 500 metres (547 yards) from where she was staying. She was believed to have killed herself.

Bu is suspected to have closed Jang's case prematurely without confirming her whereabouts.

According to local reports, Bu had allegedly told Jang's boyfriend that he had spoken to Jang over the phone and she had told Bu she did not wish to speak to her boyfriend.

Police also found the body of a man in his 60s from Jeju City on Saturday.

The man had gone missing on 28 June. Bu had closed his case and reportedly told the family that the man was found "safe" but "does not wish to disclose his location to the family".

"We believed the police when they said my father was safe and waited, but after 51 days, what returned was his body," the man's son told reporters.

It is not yet clear whether Bu was involved in the missing persons cases for two other bodies that were found in coastal villages in recent days.

Police are now examining all the missing persons reports that Bu had handled, which number nearly 300.

Jeju is one of South Korea's most popular tourist destinations.

The island, known for its rows of palm trees and sparkling waters, received more than 13 million foreign and domestic visitors last year.

While violent crime is rare in South Korea, suicide rates are among the highest in the world.

Some experts have said the low crime rate is part of the reason why missing persons cases are not taken seriously.

"After experiencing on the field that the absolute majority of missing adults are found quickly, [the officers] tend to assume all cases are like that," Lee Yung-hyeock, a professor specialising in police science at Konkuk University, told Yonhap news agency.

While more than 70,000 adults are reported missing in South Korea each year, 99% of them are marked as resolved within a month.

On Tuesday, President Lee said during a Cabinet meeting that "the recent breakdown in police discipline and irresponsibility in public safety matters have become serious problems".

Pointing out that the police are likely to wield the most power out of all the state's institutions, he said "the Korean people are questioning whether [the police] deserve this large power".

South Korea's national police chief was grilled by lawmakers at an emergency National Assembly hearing on Monday, during which he admitted that "there is a fault in the system".

This scandal comes at a politically sensitive time for South Korea's police.

The government had recently passed reform to transfer full investigative power from the prosecutors to the police, a move they said was intended to curtail the prosecutors' influence in politics.

However, the reform has been unpopular among the public, who have for many years accused the police of corruption and incompetence.

With reporting by Hosu Lee and Leehyun Choi in Seoul

articles.title: Kriti Sanon Rakhi ad: Giva jewellery drops Bollywood actor's Indian festival ad over outfit
articles.summary: Kriti Sanon has defended the ad in which she was seen celebrating the upcoming Hindu festival of Rakhi.
articles.body:
An Indian jewellery brand has removed their new advertisement for the upcoming festival of Rakshabandhan, also known as Rakhi, after backlash over the outfit worn by the female lead.

The ad featured popular Bollywood actor Kriti Sanon celebrating the Hindu festival in which sisters tie a thread called Rakhi over their brothers' wrists.

Sanon, who is seen in a cropped top, skirt and a cape, addressed her critics on Tuesday night saying "culture and traditions are in a woman's heart, not in her neckline!"

The row started earlier on Tuesday after actor and BJP MP Kangana Ranaut called the ad "intentionally creepy" and asked why someone would tie a Rakhi dressed in a bikini.

In her comments posted on social media, Ranaut did not name Sanon, but appeared to be referring to the actor.

"It is a wonderful time to be a woman, our closets are full of variety of clothes... From all the options that are available to us today why would you tie your brother a Rakhi in your bikini/under garments? Where are all your styling options? The advert looks intentionally creepy," she wrote.

Her remarks quickly drew attention online, with some users echoing her criticism of Sanon's outfit saying it was too revealing and inappropriate for a traditional festival.

One commentator described her top as a bralette, saying there was a "clear line between modern styling and basic sensitivity towards Hindu festivals".

"Pairing a bralette outfit with a sacred occasion like Rakshabandhan felt completely out of touch and unnecessary," she posted on X.

Others objected to a scene in the advertisement in which the actor also ties a rakhi on her pet dog.

But Sanon also received support, including from Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, who defended her, saying what a woman chose to wear was her own decision. Others accused Ranaut of moral policing.

Some also pointed out that though Ranaut has been more conservative in her clothing in recent years after becoming a politician, she herself often wore short dresses and Western outfits in her films and at social gatherings.

Sanon responded to the critics in an Instagram story, calling out the mindset that questioned women for their sartorial choices. Like Ranaut, she did not name anyone directly.

"The essence of festivals is not in the clothes you wear, it is in the emotions and meaning you hold for the traditions... When will we stop telling women what to wear?? Ethnic fashion has evolved over the years, but still a woman's respect for her culture is measured with just her clothes!! Culture & Traditions are in her heart, not in her neckline!"

Sanon also addressed the issue of tying Rakhi to her pet, saying though the festival traditionally celebrates the bond between a brother and sister, its spirit was about protecting loved ones - which, for her, included her sister and her pet.

Despite her spirited defence, jewellery company Giva announced on Wednesday it was pulling the ad.

"We have the highest regard and deep respect for Indian culture, traditions and festivals. As a brand, we have always believed in celebrating these joyous moments with the entire family and this time we wanted to extend the love and celebration to our pets," Giva said in a statement , external on Instagram.

Why India is talking about ripped jeans and knees

The Indian woman who stood up to moral policing - and won a pageant

Assam shorts: India teenager forced to cover legs with curtain at exam centre

"If our recent advertisement has inadvertently hurt the sentiments of some segments of society, that was not our intent at all. Out of respect, we have withdrawn the advertisement from all media," it added.

Giva is not the first Indian brand to withdraw an ad after criticism on social media. In 2020, popular jewellery brand Tanishq withdrew an advertisement featuring an interfaith couple after it faced right-wing backlash online.

Debates over what women should - and shouldn't - wear have also repeatedly sparked controversy in India.

Last year, a beauty pageant contestant was commended for standing up to a group of men who tried to bully her and other contestants over the skirts and western dresses they were wearing.

In 2021, there was outrage after a 19-year-old student, who turned up in shorts to take an exam, was forced to wrap a curtain around her legs after the teacher objected to her clothes.

In the same year, thousands of women - and some men - shared photos of themselves wearing ripped jeans after the chief minister of the northern state of Uttarakhand criticised a woman for wearing them.

articles.title: 'Become capitalists, raise money': Singer's 'advice' to Zohran Mamdani amid Bhagwat US event row
articles.summary: India News: US singer Mary Millben, who performed Indiaâs national anthem during Prime Minister Narendra Modiâs state visit to the United States in June 2023, on .
articles.body: US singer Mary Millben, who performed Indiaâs national anthem during Prime Minister Narendra Modiâs state visit to the United States in June 2023, on Tuesday (local time) criticised New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani over his opposition to an upcoming event by RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat in the city.Mamdani has been critical of Indiaâs ruling BJP and Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The RSS is the BJPâs ideological mentor.Taking to X, Millben said the mayor and other âsocialist nutsâ oppose Bhagwatâs programme solely because of their opposition to PM Modi and the BJP.âGiven these nuts subscribe to the ideology of socialism, they donât understand capitalism. MSG doesnât answer to socialist rants. They answer to capitalism. And thus this event will go on because of it,â she wrote.She further challenged Mamdani and his âchoir of socialistsâ to rent the iconic Madison Square Garden (MSG), where Bhagwatâs event is scheduled to be held, and organise their own rally for their âanti-Modi foolishness.âThe US singer also expressed support for the central theme of the event while calling for constructive dialogue: "Side note, I like the rally title. 'Oneness'. We are ONE family. I hope this rally includes meaningful dialogue on religious freedom in India," she noted.Millbenâs comments came after Mamdani, New York Cityâs first Muslim and Indian-American mayor, said on Tuesday that he does not support the planned August 29 event at Madison Square Garden, where Bhagwat is scheduled to address members of the Indian diaspora. He, however, noted that city authorities may not have the legal authority to stop the event, describing it as a âprivate gathering."âI don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on cancelling a private event,â Mamdani said at a press conference when asked whether municipal authorities should move to cancel it.He added: âMy mother's family is all still in India... And it has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision of any country, frankly, and so it is one that I find myself in deep opposition to, not only as an Indian-American but also as the mayor of a city that believes deeply in the belonging of each and every person, no matter their colour, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from.âBhagwatâs New York visit is the first leg of a three-nation global outreach tour covering the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom. The tour has been organised at the invitation of overseas local groups as part of the RSSâs centenary celebrations.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: GPS cannot work everywhere, so scientists tested a new navigation system that uses Cosmic rays instead of satellites to make it work under water and rocks
articles.summary: Tech News News: GPS has become essential for navigation. But there is one major limitation: GPS signals cannot travel through water, rocks or deep underground spaces..
articles.body: GPS has become essential for navigation. But there is one major limitation: GPS signals cannot travel through water, rocks or deep underground spaces. To address the problem, scientists in Japan are now testing an alternative navigation system that uses particles from cosmic rays instead of satellites. According to a report by Ars Technica, the system is called the Muometric Wireless Navigation System, or MuWNS. It uses naturally occurring particles known as muons to determine location in places where GPS cannot work, including underground, indoors and underwater.The researchers say the technology could one day help guide robots during search and rescue operations, support autonomous vehicles in underground spaces and improve navigation in places where satellite signals are unavailable.How cosmic rays could help navigation work underground and underwaterCosmic rays constantly produce particles called muons that fall across the Earth. Unlike GPS radio signals, muons can pass through dense materials, including water and large amounts of rock.âCosmic ray muons fall evenly across the Earth and always travel at the same speed no matter what material they pass through, penetrating even kilometers of rock,â Hiroyuki Tanaka of the University of Tokyo said.âNow, using muons, weâve developed a new type of GPS, which weâve called muPS, that works underground, indoors, and underwater.âThe technology works by using reference stations placed above ground along with a receiver that detects muons below the surface. By measuring the particles and using synchronized clocks, the system can calculate the location of the receiver.Muon technology is not entirely new. Scientists have previously used muons to study volcanoes, examine ancient structures and search for hidden spaces inside pyramids. The Japanese researchers are now exploring whether the same particles can help solve a different problem: navigation without satellite signals.Scientists tested the system by walking through a building basementEarlier versions of the system required the receiver to be connected to a ground station with wires, limiting where it could be used. The new MuWNS system is wireless and uses accurate quartz clocks to synchronize the reference stations and receiver.For a test, researchers placed reference stations on the sixth floor of a building while a person carrying the receiver walked through corridors in the basement. The system tracked the person's route and was able to reconstruct the path taken.The researchers reported an accuracy of between 2 and 25 metres, with a range of up to 100 metres.âThis is as good as, if not better than, single-point GPS positioning over the ground in urban areas,â Tanaka said. However, he added that the technology is still far from being ready for everyday use. âPeople need an accuracy of one meter, and the key to that is time synchronization.âGet the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Far-right Israeli lawmaker damages Palestinian memorial with sledgehammer
articles.summary: Zvi Sukkot's actions have drawn widespread condemnation, including from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
articles.body:
A far-right member of the Israeli parliament has badly damaged a Palestinian memorial with a sledgehammer in the occupied West Bank while under military escort.

The incident has drawn strong criticism from Palestinians and across the political spectrum in Israel.

Video footage showed Zvi Sukkot, a member of the far-right Religious Zionism party, and several others striking the stone memorial in the Palestinian village of Madama.

In the video, Sukkot - who has a history of provocative anti-Palestinian acts - says: "This is something we cannot leave standing here, because any place that glorifies terrorism, we must remove it."

Rami Nasar, the head of the village council in Madama, said that the monument was erected in 2008 to remember Palestinians killed in the battle of Karameh - a day-long military confrontation between Israeli forces and those of both the PLO and Jordan in 1968.

It also memorialises Palestinians killed in the first and second intifada.

Nasar said it was intended to honour those who had been killed in conflict with Israel, whatever their political affiliation.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said its soldiers had been present during the incident. The Israeli military said it had approved a tour of monuments in the area for Sukkot and was providing security.

But the IDF said he and the others involved had acted deceptively and without authorisation.

It said soldiers eventually stopped Sukkot and escorted his group out of Madama after reporting the incident to their commanders.

In a number of previous incidents involving settler violence, soldiers have been filmed standing by without intervening.

The incident has further raised the temperature in the West Bank, where increasing attacks by settlers on Palestinians in recent months have drawn international condemnation.

Madama itself has been the target of several attacks by settlers.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office has issued a statement criticising Sukkot's actions. It read: "Taking the law into one's own hands, especially when it involves public figures, is a reprehensible practice that prevents the IDF from focusing on its missions of combating terrorism and incitement to violence."

Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming general election, Gadi Eisenkot, said that Sukkot's behaviour was "a disgrace for anyone who claims to represent the public and be a leader".

Eisenkot also criticised Netanyahu for "allowing anarchists like Zvi Sukkot and his ilk to do whatever they please, endangering security in the settlements and harming Israel's standing in the world".

But finance minister Bezalel Smotrich - who heads the Religious Zionism party to which Sukkot belongs - directed his fiercest criticism at what he called the "frantic rush of the left-wing opposition to condemn Sukkot rather than terrorism itself".

On Monday, the most senior Israeli military officer in the West Bank, Major General Avi Bluth, was reported by Israeli media to have told Netanyahu in a closed-door meeting that the mounting violence by settlers could ignite a major escalation.

The incident has drawn strong criticism from Palestinians and across the political spectrum in Israel.
Video footage showed Zvi Sukkot, a member of the far-right Religious Zionism party, and several others striking the stone memorial in the Palestinian village of Madama.
In the video, Sukkot - who has a history of provocative anti-Palestinian acts - says: "This is something we cannot leave standing here, because any place that glorifies terrorism, we must remove it."

Rami Nasar, the head of the village council in Madama, said that the monument was erected in 2008 to remember Palestinians killed in the battle of Karameh - a day-long military confrontation between Israeli forces and those of both the PLO and Jordan in 1968.
It also memorialises Palestinians killed in the first and second intifada.
Nasar said it was intended to honour those who had been killed in conflict with Israel, whatever their political affiliation.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said its soldiers had been present during the incident. The Israeli military said it had approved a tour of monuments in the area for Sukkot and was providing security.
But the IDF said he and the others involved had acted deceptively and without authorisation.
It said soldiers eventually stopped Sukkot and escorted his group out of Madama after reporting the incident to their commanders.
In a number of previous incidents involving settler violence, soldiers have been filmed standing by without intervening.
The incident has further raised the temperature in the West Bank, where increasing attacks by settlers on Palestinians in recent months have drawn international condemnation.
Madama itself has been the target of several attacks by settlers.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office has issued a statement criticising Sukkot's actions. It read: "Taking the law into one's own hands, especially when it involves public figures, is a reprehensible practice that prevents the IDF from focusing on its missions of combating terrorism and incitement to violence."
Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming general election, Gadi Eisenkot, said that Sukkot's behaviour was "a disgrace for anyone who claims to represent the public and be a leader".

Eisenkot also criticised Netanyahu for "allowing anarchists like Zvi Sukkot and his ilk to do whatever they please, endangering security in the settlements and harming Israel's standing in the world".

But finance minister Bezalel Smotrich - who heads the Religious Zionism party to which Sukkot belongs - directed his fiercest criticism at what he called the "frantic rush of the left-wing opposition to condemn Sukkot rather than terrorism itself".

On Monday, the most senior Israeli military officer in the West Bank, Major General Avi Bluth, was reported by Israeli media to have told Netanyahu in a closed-door meeting that the mounting violence by settlers could ignite a major escalation.

articles.title: Haiti gang raid death toll rises to 47 as more than 50 kidnapped, says UN
articles.summary: UN chief Guterres said the attack underscores ‘the alarming security situation in Haiti’ due to gangs.
articles.body:
At least 47 people were killed, more than 50 others kidnapped, and another 22 people injured in a gang raid near Haiti’s capital of Port-au-Prince, the United Nations has said, prompting anger over violence amid repeated deadly attacks.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday condemned the attack in the town of Kenscoff, which took place on the evening of August 23 .

list 1 of 4 UN chief blames global indifference for Haiti crisis

list 2 of 4 A lifetime in the making: Haitians in the US celebrate World Cup return

list 3 of 4 Will the end of TPS for Haitians mean a caregiving crisis in US?

list 4 of 4 Brutal gang attack on strategic Haiti hillside leaves at least 30 dead

It is believed to be one of the largest mass kidnappings in Haiti in recent years, and comes as Haiti hopes to hold its first general election in more than a decade.

Guterres said in a statement that the event underscores “the alarming security situation in Haiti and reinforce[s] the urgent need to intensify Haitian and international security efforts to combat gangs”.

Jean Massillon, Kenscoff’s mayor, said armed men “sowed chaos” as they set homes on fire and killed residents. He said gang members targeted a church and homes, including that of Jean William Pape, a leading public health expert.

Massillon blamed the attack on members of Viv Ansanm, a group that was designated as a “foreign terrorist organisation” by the United States government last year.

The United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti has said estimates of casualties could change.

Even as Haiti’s government decried a “heinous attack” and promised to reinforce security, residents demanded the local police chief step down, saying officers failed to protect people killed a short distance from the police station.

Kenscoff resident Marc Paul, 42, said gangs kidnapped his brother, stepmother, stepfather and two cousins. He said his 16-year-old niece was also captured and raped but was able to escape and has reunited with him.

“I had to run over bodies,” he told The Associated Press news agency as he recalled how he fled the attack.

Another resident, Coriolan Kendy, standing by his cousin’s body, lying on the road in a blood-stained sheet, told the Reuters news agency: “People in Kenscoff are suffering and the government is to blame.”

The prime minister’s office has promised to take action, stating that “Kenscoff will not be abandoned”.

“The government’s authority will be restored, without weakness and without delay,’ the prime minister’s office said on social media.

In a video posted on social media, a gang leader threatened Vladimir Paraison, director of the Haitian National Police.

“Paraison, if any of our soldiers are hurt, I will kill all of them,” he said, referring to the hostages.

The gang member identified himself as Izo 2, a reference to Izo, or Johnson Andre, one of Haiti’s most powerful gang leaders.

The hillside community of Kenscoff, in a strategic position overlooking routes into the capital, has suffered a dozen attacks by armed gangs since last year, forcing thousands to flee their homes.

Powerful gangs under a broad alliance have for years cemented their influence over Haiti’s capital and expanded to nearby regions, despite attempts by foreign nations to reinforce the country’s outgunned police.

articles.title: US immigration agents arrested more than 49,500 people in July
articles.summary: The number of arrests last month showed a rise of roughly 15 percent over June’s count.
articles.body:
United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested 49,571 people in July, the highest in a month since President Donald Trump took office for his second term, according to the latest figures available.

The figures for July showed a rise of roughly 15 percent over June’s count and about 70 percent above February’s total, according to government data provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project based at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of California, Los Angeles and analysed by The Associated Press news agency.

list 1 of 3 Most Americans say Trump has gone too far on US immigration: Poll

list 2 of 3 US plans to equip ICE officers with electric-shock gloves

list 3 of 3 Salvadoran man dies in ICE custody at New Jersey detention centre

The month before Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025, monthly arrests were slightly more than 8,000, a figure largely made up of immigrants transferred from city or state jails and prisons and turned over to ICE to remove from the country.

In his first year back in office, the monthly numbers started climbing as officials eased limits on where and whom agents could target. By December, monthly arrests had surpassed 40,000.

In the aftermath of two fatal shootings in Minnesota in January that led to protests and an uproar from Democratic lawmakers, arrests began to fall in February. After remaining stagnant for months, the numbers surged in June and then again in July.

Nearly 20,000 of the July arrests happened in Texas and Florida. Both states have taken part in cooperation deals with ICE known as 287(g) agreements that enable local law enforcement to essentially operate as additional arms for immigration enforcement.

The expanding arrest campaign comes after a hiring drive, with ICE bringing on roughly 12,000 additional officers and agents last year.

articles.title: In 1968, the Netherlands reclaimed land from the sea for factories; when the development was abandoned, birds colonised it and the accidental wetland became a 56-square-kilometre nature reserve
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover the transformation of a 1968 abandoned industrial site into the thriving Oostvaardersplassen nature reserve, showcasing how ecological recovery can reshape landscapes and support biodiversity.
articles.body: In 1968, Dutch engineers drained a stretch of the IJsselmeer near Lelystad to create new land meant for factories and warehouses, a history recorded on the official site page kept by Nationaal Park Nieuw Land. The industrial estate was never built. The abandoned ground filled with rainwater and seepage, wild geese settled on it within a few seasons, and the site gradually became the Oostvaardersplassen, a wetland that now covers 56 square kilometres and draws researchers from across Europe.Part of a much larger Dutch programme to reclaim land from the old Zuiderzee for farms, housing and industry, the reserve lies within the Zuidelijk Flevoland polder. Planners expected the newly drained ground near Lelystad to carry factories once the clay soil had settled enough to build on. Workers sowed reeds across the marshy sections to stop that soil from shifting during the wait. The construction that was meant to follow never arrived, largely because the oil crisis of the 1970s slowed the wider Dutch economy and left the planned industrial estate on paper only. With no bulldozers on site, the reed beds and shallow pools simply carried on spreading through the wet clay. That gap between plan and outcome makes the Oostvaardersplassen unusual among nature reserves. Almost nowhere else in Europe did a protected wetland begin life as a rejected industrial park rather than a landscape someone set out to conserve.Geese arrived before officials changed their mindsGreylag geese found the marshy ground long before any government body decided what to do with it. Their grazing kept young willow and reed growth in check, which stopped the site from turning into scrubby woodland and instead let open water and reed beds spread further. That habitat pulled in a growing list of migratory birds, from spoonbills to great white egrets, along with species that had grown scarce elsewhere in the Netherlands.A group of ecologists led by Frans Vera noticed what was happening and began pushing for the site to be protected rather than eventually drained for the industry it was originally meant to hold. Their case succeeded. By 1983 the site had been formally designated a nature reserve by Staatsbosbeheer, the Dutch state forestry service, and in 1989 it earned recognition as a Wetland of International Importance, a status confirmed in the site record kept by the Ramsar Sites Information Service and normally reserved for wetlands with long, well-documented ecological histories rather than ones barely two decades old.From accidental swamp to a rewilding case studyOnce protected, the Oostvaardersplassen became a live experiment rather than a conventional park. Vera and the management team introduced Heck cattle, Konik horses and red deer to graze alongside the geese, aiming to recreate the kind of open, herbivore-shaped landscape that may have covered parts of prehistoric Europe. Left largely without supplementary feeding, the herds bred, competed for food and thinned out in hard winters much as wild populations would. That management approach was the subject of an in-depth account carried by Ecos.That approach has not been free of controversy. Harsh winters have periodically killed large numbers of grazing animals, prompting public debate in the Netherlands over how much human intervention a wild reserve should allow. Independent panels have since pushed for more active management of herd numbers, and rules around supplementary feeding have shifted more than once in response.The site has also grown in size and status since its early years. It became part of Nieuw Land National Park when that park was established in 2018, joining neighbouring dune and marsh areas under a single protected designation. Visitors can now walk marked trails along the reserve's edges and watch herds of horses and cattle roam ground that was originally planned for warehouses and loading docks. What began as surplus polder, too wet and too unstable for the factories it was drained for, is today one of the most closely watched rewilding sites in Europe, offering scientists a rare long-term record of how quickly wild habitat can reclaim ground that humans once carved out of the sea for entirely different purposes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Dog treat founder eats her own products, even packs them in her kids' lunches
articles.summary: In celebration of National Dog Day, Lord Jameson's founder says the MAHA movement should extend to pets with organic, whole-food treats free of artificial additives.
articles.body: It's National Dog Day, and one dog treat creator thinks dogs should be included in the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiative, which emphasizes whole, nutrient-dense foods. "We have never used anything artificial," Sarah Goldberger, New York-based founder and CEO of organic dog treat company Lord Jameson, told Fox News Digital.  "We've never used fake food coloring. We've never used fake flavoring. All of our bright, beautiful colors come from real fruits and vegetables." CHEAP, HEALTHY FOOD IS REJECTED BY MOST AMERICANS EVEN AS MAHA MOVEMENT PUSHES IT Since becoming an official federal initiative in February 2025, the MAHA Commission has promoted a greater focus on whole, nutrient-dense foods while calling for reductions in refined carbohydrates, added sugars and certain artificial additives. Goldberger believes those nutritional priorities will "translate into the pet space." "My hope is that as a brand, we can inspire other pet brands to make better choices to really impact the lives and the health and wellness of dogs," she said. Goldberger started Lord Jameson in 2019, inspired by her late dog, Jameson, after noticing what she described as a void in the market for healthier dog treats. HERE'S WHY DOGS DON'T NEED 'HUMAN FOOD,' SAYS VIRGINIA VETERINARIAN: 'NO REASON FOR IT' "Jameson had gone through a pretty serious medical issue, and the medication he was being given actually created toxicity in his body," Goldberger said.  Goldberger said she wanted to offer treats made with "completely clean ingredients, organic, gluten-free, no preservatives, no toxins, no artificial colors or flavors." "So we started working with a homeopathic vet, and we were reminded of the power of plant-based medicine. A lot of the formulas, especially in our wellness products, are meant to serve dogs during a time of needed healing with plant-based products, more herbs and botanicals." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS When she set out to create the brand, Goldberger said she surveyed more than 1,000 pet parents and found that many reported their dogs had allergies or sensitivities to various animal proteins, preservatives and food colorings. Goldberger said she wanted to offer treats made with "completely clean ingredients, organic, gluten-free, no preservatives, no toxins, no artificial colors or flavors." Despite not using preservatives, the treats have an 18-month shelf life, which Goldberger said is "very difficult to achieve in production" and is "another key selling point for us." Lord Jameson, Goldberger said, has "truly reimagined what dog treats can be and should be." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER She said she eats the treats herself and even puts them in her children's lunchboxes. They've been a hit with pet owners for a variety of reasons, including what Goldberger described as their effect on dogs' digestive systems. "As a dog mom myself, I know the frustration when you go to the store, you buy food or a treat, you bring it home and all of a sudden they have diarrhea," she said.  "Because we're using whole-food ingredients and no preservatives, you're going to get a nice firm poop after they eat. It sounds funny to say, but this is something you'll see in a lot of our reviews." Goldberger also said the treats can be suitable for some dogs with colitis, diabetes or other specialized dietary needs. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Lord Jameson has since launched a line of "protein-inspired" flavors as part of its Love Puffs line, made with organic sorghum, a whole grain that contains protein and fiber. Another feature that sets Lord Jameson apart, Goldberger said, is that the brand is "completely vertically integrated," with its manufacturing operations, including its kitchen, warehouse and fulfillment center, based in Boulder, Colorado. "We've had no price increase for three or four years, no issues with any tariffs because everything is sourced primarily in North America," Goldberger said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lord Jameson treats are sold at 5,500 independent pet retailers in the United States, as well as at some grocery stores, and are available internationally in four countries. Kelly McGreal of Fox News Digital contributed to this report.

articles.title: Australia to hand-vaccinate 5,000 wild penguins against bird flu spreading across wildlife; the birdsâ nightly routine will make the daunting task possible
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Australia is launching a necessary effort to protect one of its most recognisable coastal birds from H5N1 bird flu. Wildlife teams are hand-vaccinatin.
articles.body: Australia is launching a necessary effort to protect one of its most recognisable coastal birds from H5N1 bird flu. Wildlife teams are hand-vaccinating thousands of wild little penguins. On Phillip Island, Victoria, authorities hope to protect a colony of about 5,000 birds by catching them as they return to their burrows after feeding at sea. The operation comes as concern grows over the virus spreading beyond birds. SBS News reported that a second seal in South Australia was suspected of having bird flu, just a day after the country confirmed its first mammal case. The vaccination campaign is being carried out at night and is designed around the penguinsâ remarkably predictable routine. For the tiny birds, that familiar evening journey could now offer the best chance of avoiding a potentially devastating outbreak during the dangerous season ahead.Ambitious target to hand-vaccinate 5,000 penguinsThe answer lies in the little penguinsâ daily routine. Unlike many wild animals, little penguins return to their burrows at roughly the same time each evening. After spending the day at sea hunting for food, they come ashore around sunset and follow familiar routes back towards their colonies. That predictable behaviour makes it possible for wildlife workers to intercept them. SBS News reported that teams have been working late into the night to improve the process. They initially worked along quieter penguin pathways to learn how to handle the birds efficiently before moving to the western end of the penguin parade, where larger numbers return. By the weekend, another 600 penguins had been vaccinated, bringing the number that had received a first dose at Phillip Island and St Kilda to about 1,000.The birds are caught as they return from their daily trips to sea. They are then vaccinated, microchipped and released back towards their burrows. The entire operation is carried out at night, when the penguins naturally gather. It is an extraordinary amount of work for such small animals. Yet their habits make the task considerably more practical than trying to vaccinate other free-ranging species.Why are Australian authorities vaccinating wild penguinsThe little penguin population on Phillip Island is facing a serious new threat from H5N1, a highly contagious form of bird flu. The island is home to around 40,000 little penguins, while the specific vaccination effort is focused on about 5,000 birds. As per âA-Z Animals,â Victoriaâs programme is intended to become the worldâs largest vaccination campaign targeting wild birds. Each penguin needs two separate doses, meaning the same birds have to be caught twice. Officials also plan to microchip the birds so they can identify which penguins have received their injections.The need for action has become more urgent after H5N1 was detected among little penguins. A-Z Animals reported that one penguin on Phillip Island had already died from the virus shortly before the vaccination programme began. The danger is not limited to the birds. SBS News notes that five suspected H5 bird flu cases were recorded in South Australia on 24 August, including a long-nosed fur seal at The Pages Conservation Park. The animal was being tested, with results expected in the following days. That came just one day after Australia confirmed its first mammal case of a long-nosed fur seal at Beachport, about 300 kilometres south of Adelaide. Authorities believed that the seal had contracted the virus from wild birds.Little penguins are perfect for this unique operationWildlife vaccination is extremely difficult because animals move freely and can be hard to locate repeatedly. Little penguins offer several advantages. According to A-Z Animals, penguins live in colonies, return to the same burrows each evening and cannot fly away. Their predictable movements mean workers have a realistic opportunity to catch the same birds more than once. Phillip Islandâs famous penguin parade also means the birds are accustomed to people being nearby. Hundreds of thousands of visitors come to the island each year to watch the penguins make their evening return. Their familiarity with humans can make it easier for wildlife teams to work quickly while causing less disruption. For the conservation teams, that behaviour could make the difference between a vaccination programme that sounds impossible and one that can actually be carried out.How serious could an H5N1 outbreak becomeThe potential consequences are significant because Phillip Island supports the world's largest little penguin colony. Australian government modelling from May 2025 estimated that a worst-case H5N1 outbreak could kill between 8,000 and 16,000 little penguins on Phillip Island alone. articles.title: A Scottish scholar and his American wife bought the remote island of Canna; 43 years later they gifted it, their home and their lifeâs work preserving Gaelic culture to the National Trust for Scotland
articles.summary: UK News: John Lorne Campbell and Margaret Fay Shaw had already spent years recording Gaelic songs, stories and traditions when they made the remote Isle of Can.
articles.body: John Lorne Campbell and Margaret Fay Shaw had already spent years recording Gaelic songs, stories and traditions when they made the remote Isle of Canna their home in 1938. The Scottish folklorists continued that work from the island for more than four decades before Campbell gifted Canna, their home, library, archives and sound recordings to the National Trust for Scotland.According to the Trust, Campbell was born in Argyll on October 1, 1906. The eldest son of Colonel Duncan Campbell of Inverneill and his American wife, Ethel Waterbury of New Jersey, he was educated at Cargilfield School in Edinburgh and Rugby. He later studied Rural Economy at St Johnâs College, Oxford, as well as Celtic under Professor John Fraser of Jesus College.His interest in Gaelic had started in childhood and grew during his time at Oxford. With the help of Fraser, who became his mentor, Campbell began working on a Gaelic anthology. His first published book, Highland Songs of the Forty-Five, appeared in 1933.That same year, his work took him to the Outer Hebrides. He arrived on Barra on August 4, 1933, to study crofting conditions and colloquial Gaelic. The visit became the beginning of a long effort to collect and preserve Gaelic songs, stories and linguistic records.From Barra to CannaOn Barra, Campbell became involved with local people and explored the Gaelic traditions of the Hebrides. He started with an Ediphone Recorder using wax cylinders and later moved to a Presto Disc Recorder. He obtained both in New York and used equipment that was considered state-of-the-art at the time.Campbell also travelled to eastern Canada, particularly Cape Breton, to study Gaelic traditions among the descendants of 18th- and 19th-century emigrants. He found that Gaelic oral traditions were still alive after more than 100 years of separation from Scotland.In 1937, while in Nova Scotia, he also recorded the history and traditions of the Micmac Indians, the Indigenous people of the Maritime Provinces. He described Cape Breton as 'a Highland Community where there are no lairds'.Campbellâs life took another major turn in 1938 when he bought the islands of Canna and Sanday. He and Margaret moved to Canna after spending three years living on Barra.Campbell had met Margaret Fay Shaw in South Uist in 1934, where she was collecting traditional Gaelic songs. Margaretâs musical talents and Campbellâs knowledge of words and language, built what became a major collection of Gaelic cultural material.The couple lived at Canna House, which had been built around 1863 by Donald Macneil, who owned the island at the time. The house and island were later sold to Greenock shipowner Robert Thom in 1881. His family remained there until his death in 1911, after which the island was eventually bought by Campbell.Canna House became both their home and a place where they continued their research. Campbell spent long hours in its library transcribing and archiving his Gaelic recordings and writing academic works. Margaret continued her own work through photography and film.The 1981 giftIn 1981, Campbell presented Canna to the National Trust for Scotland. The gift included Canna House, the island, his library, archives and sound recordings. Campbell and Margaret continued living there and devoted their time to cataloguing and publishing their research.The National Trust for Scotland says the collection inside Canna House is of international importance. It includes material covering Gaelic folk songs and tales, Celtic and Norse studies, philology, music, literature and Scottish history.The archives also preserve Margaretâs photographic collection of more than 6,000 images from the early 20th century in the Hebrides. Campbellâs work includes 1,700 sound recordings, his Hebridean Lepidoptera collection and the research writings collected by the couple over about 60 years.The house also retains their furnishings, artworks and personal belongings, giving a record of the life they built around their research.Their work continues Campbell died suddenly on April 25, 1996, while on holiday at Villa San Girolamo in Fiesole, Italy. He had asked to be buried where he died, and he was initially interred there. In 2006, his remains were reinterred on Canna, in the bluebell woods he had planted as a young man. Margaret died in 2004. Their work, however, remained connected to Canna House through the collections they had built and preserved there.Magda Sagarzazu, who had known the Campbells closely, continued Campbellâs work after his death. She had first come to Canna from the Basque Country in 1960, aged 11, with her sister and father. She spent much of her childhood on the island and developed a close bond with the Campbells, particularly John.After Campbell died, Magda lived with Margaret at Canna House and continued cataloguing and documenting his archive of papers and books until she retired in 2015.Today, Canna House is open for pre-booked guided tours. Visitors can see rooms including the library, where Campbell worked, and Margaret Fay Shawâs study, which contains examples of her work in photography and film. Her Graflex camera is also displayed there, while a projector shows film footage of everyday life on Canna and South Uist.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Next Atlantic storm to be named 'Dolly' in an uncanny 'coincidence'
articles.summary: US News: The death of country music icon Dolly Parton has created an unusual coincidence in the Atlantic: the next tropical storm to form there is set to be ca.
articles.body: The death of country music icon Dolly Parton has created an unusual coincidence in the Atlantic: the next tropical storm to form there is set to be called Dolly. The timing is striking, but the overlap is entirely coincidental.Dolly had been on the predetermined 2026 Atlantic storm list years before Partonâs death. It appears on a list maintained under procedures established by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and was never chosen as a tribute to the singer.Atlantic storm names are drawn from rotating lists that are reused every six years unless a name is later retired. The system is established in advance so storms can be identified quickly and consistently once they reach the required strength, the news agency Associated Press reported.A coincidence written into the hurricane list years agoUnlike names chosen for commemorative events, tropical cyclone names are fixed well before a hurricane season begins.For the Atlantic, the WMO maintains predetermined lists of names that are used sequentially as qualifying storms develop. The names alternate between male and female, and the lists generally return on a six-year cycle unless individual names are removed.The system also serves a practical purpose. Giving storms distinct names allows meteorologists, emergency agencies, broadcasters and the public to follow individual weather systems more easily, particularly when several are active at the same time.How a storm earns the name DollyBeing next on the list does not mean the name Dolly is guaranteed to be used.For a tropical or subtropical cyclone to receive a name, it must reach tropical-storm strength, with maximum sustained winds of at least 39 mph (63 kph).If the next qualifying Atlantic system reaches that threshold, forecasters would assign it the next unused name on the 2026 list â Dolly.The name is therefore tied to the predetermined sequence of storms during the season, not to events involving any person who happens to share it.The system that could put the name into useThe National Hurricane Center (NHC) is watching disturbed weather in the eastern tropical Atlantic, south of the Cabo Verde Islands, where conditions could support further development.The system would first need to become sufficiently organised to be classified as a tropical depression. Only if it subsequently strengthens to tropical-storm intensity would the name Dolly come into use.That outcome remains uncertain, but the name is next in line because the Atlantic has already used the first three names designated for 2026.Those were Arthur, Bertha and Cristobal. Arthur affected the US Gulf Coast in June, Bertha brought heavy rain to parts of Louisiana and Texas in July, and Cristobal became the seasonâs third named storm in August before weakening.Their progression leaves Dolly as the fourth available name on this yearâs list.When storm names disappear for goodWhile Atlantic storm-name lists normally return every six years, some names never come back.Names associated with particularly deadly or destructive storms can be permanently retired from the rotating lists. The practice prevents names strongly associated with catastrophic events from being used again in future seasons.That happened after the 2025 season with Melissa, a Category 5 hurricane that caused extensive destruction across the Caribbean and killed more than 90 people.Melissa was formally retired in 2026. When that list returns in 2031, the replacement name will be Molly.The process illustrates how storm names can acquire powerful associations only after they are used. Dolly, by contrast, remains simply the next predetermined name waiting on the 2026 list.A quieter Atlantic season in 2026The potential emergence of Dolly comes during a hurricane season that NOAA says is now most likely to finish with below-normal activity.In its updated August outlook, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) placed the probability of a below-normal Atlantic season at 75%, up from 55% in its preseason assessment.NOAA now forecasts seven to 13 named storms for the full season, including two to six hurricanes and zero to two major hurricanes.El NiÃ±o is one factor behind that outlook. It tends to increase vertical wind shear over the Atlantic, making conditions less favourable for tropical systems to develop and strengthen.Whether the disturbance south of Cabo Verde develops far enough to become Tropical Storm Dolly is still an open question. The coincidence with Partonâs death may be remarkable, but the name itself was settled years before the events of this week.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
