articles.title: In 1925, New Yorker Gayer Dominick bought Bulls Island as a private hunting preserve; 11 years later he gave it to Cape Romain refuge for seabirds and shorebirds
articles.summary: US News: Discover the fascinating history of Bulls Island, from its purchase by banker Gayer Dominick in 1925 to its transformation into a vital national wildlife refuge, supporting over 290 bird species.
articles.body: For 229 years, ownership of Bulls Island, a wild barrier island off the coast of South Carolina that is now part of Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge, passed through 36 different private hands, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, which records that the island had 36 private owners from 1696 to 1936. The island and surrounding refuge now support more than 290 recorded bird species, with FWS documentation listing over 293 bird species in Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge. Then a wealthy New York banker bought it, built a mansion on it, and eventually turned it over to the federal government for good, setting the stage for a major shorebird refuge on the East Coast.Dominick purchases Bull Island as its 36th private owner since 1696Gayer Dominick, a New York banker and stockbroker with a passion for hunting, purchased Bull Island in 1925, according to reporting by the Post and Courier. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service records that he bought the island with the specific intent of turning it into a private hunting preserve. The refugeâs own visitor records say Dominick was the islandâs 36th private owner and this part of the chain of ownership goes back to 1696. Over roughly 240 years, Bulls Island changed hands repeatedly before Dominick eventually transferred it to the federal government. By the time Dominick arrived, Bulls Island had already lived through centuries of use.Dominick builds a sky-blue mansion and strings electricity across the Island Dominick had a large house built on the island soon after buying it, a sprawling structure that came to be known as Dominick House. The Post and Courier reports that Dominick was wealthy enough to string electric wires from island to island to power his retreat, at a time when only about half of all Americans, urban and rural combined, had electricity at all, though the great majority of urban households were already electrified by the mid-1920s. He also paid to have heavy equipment shipped in by boat so roads could be cut through the island's maritime forest, a level of investment beyond what most of the island's previous owners had been able or willing to undertake. The house Dominick built still stands today and Discover South Carolina notes that it later operated for years as an inn catering to visiting fishermen, birders, and other nature enthusiasts before eventually being converted into housing for refuge staff and volunteers.Outside the dwelling, Dominick's ultimate goal was altering the island's habitat features for his hunting pursuits. It was Dominickâs efforts, specifically, his alterations to Bulls Islandâs existing water impoundments to attract more waterfowl, as noted by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, that ultimately created the ecological conditions that later made the island so valuable for bird conservation. As the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has noted, Dominick's hunting-driven renovations for wetland environments created unforeseen uses far surpassing his personal agenda.Dominick Conveys Bulls Island to the Fish and Wildlife Service in 1936 Eleven years later, Dominick sold his interests (the whole island, his family's shore house and hunting cabin) to the federal government, ceding Bulls Island in 1936. The 1936 transfer added Dominickâs entire property, making Bulls Island the southernmost barrier island in the refuge, to the Cape Romain Migratory Waterfowl Refuge, which had been established in 1932 and later renamed Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge.The refuge expands to support seabirds and shorebirds along the coastCape Romain has grown in scale since Dominick made his gift. The refuge now covers more than 66,000 acres of barrier islands, salt marshes and maritime forest along South Carolinaâs southeast coast. In 1975, Congress designated 29,000 acres of the refuge as a National Wilderness Area under the Wilderness Act and the next year the refuge was designated as a Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network Site of International Importance. Bulls Island remains a popular part of the refuge, offering sanctuary to some 290 different species of bird, along with the alligators, deer and black fox squirrels who live in the same maritime forest that Dominick once hacked roads through. Visitors can still see the tabby ruins of the island's old fort and the Sewee middens, reminders of the islandâs long history before Dominickâs eleven-year ownership.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. As the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has noted, Dominick's hunting-driven renovations for wetland environments created unforeseen uses far surpassing his personal agenda.Dominick Conveys Bulls Island to the Fish and Wildlife Service in 1936 Eleven years later, Dominick sold his interests (the whole island, his family's shore house and hunting cabin) to the federal government, ceding Bulls Island in 1936. The 1936 transfer added Dominickâs entire property, making Bulls Island the southernmost barrier island in the refuge, to the Cape Romain Migratory Waterfowl Refuge, which had been established in 1932 and later renamed Cape Romain National Wildlife Refuge.The refuge expands to support seabirds and shorebirds along the coastCape Romain has grown in scale since Dominick made his gift. The refuge now covers more than 66,000 acres of barrier islands, salt marshes and maritime forest along South Carolinaâs southeast coast. In 1975, Congress designated 29,000 acres of the refuge as a National Wilderness Area under the Wilderness Act and the next year the refuge was designated as a Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network Site of International Importance. Bulls Island remains a popular part of the refuge, offering sanctuary to some 290 different species of bird, along with the alligators, deer and black fox squirrels who live in the same maritime forest that Dominick once hacked roads through. Visitors can still see the tabby ruins of the island's old fort and the Sewee middens, reminders of the islandâs long history before Dominickâs eleven-year ownership.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: The Bulgarian village that fears becoming an Iranian target
articles.summary: US Air Force refuelling planes caused anxiety in Bezmer. While their departure has brought relief, tensions persist.
articles.body:
Bezmer, Bulgaria – The news landed on Saturday, bringing relief to nearby villagers: two United States Air Force (USAF) refuelling aircraft had left Bulgaria’s Bezmer airbase.

“The USAF air tankers took off yesterday and left Bulgaria,” the country’s defence minister, Dimitar Stoyanov, announced, as President Iliana Yotova declared: “For now, this mission is over.”

list 1 of 2 NATO ‘prepared’ to defend allies amid report of Iranian strike plans

list 2 of 2 Why Iran is threatening Europe’s ‘strategically important’ southeast

The US Air Force said the Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, intended to aid Washington’s war on Iran, had left to support “other operational requirements”.

The village had spent weeks worrying that the aircraft could make their area in southeastern Bulgaria a target for Iranian attacks.

Tehran had urged Bulgaria against allowing its territory to be used for the US and Israel’s military operation against Iran. Later, citing unnamed Iranian sources, the Financial Times reported that in the event of Washington’s escalation in Iran, Iranian forces had “assessed striking US assets in southeastern European countries such as Bulgaria” after Sofia had approved the use of its Bezmer airbase for US refuelling aircraft.

“I pray to God that our village won’t be attacked,” a woman working at a local grocery shop, who requested anonymity, told Al Jazeera days before the tankers left. “We are scared, but nothing depends on us.”

Although the planes are gone, geopolitical tensions – as well as fears in Bezmer of being drawn into the US-Israel war on Iran once again – persist.

This week, Stoyanov told reporters that Iran had carried out an effective hybrid operation, aided by Bulgarian politicians in the opposition.

“Unfortunately, this hybrid operation will continue,” he predicted in comments understood to have been directed at the opposition. Stoyanov did not elaborate further.

In Bezmer, a village of about 1,000 people that sits beside the base, Bulgarian military aircraft have long been part of the landscape. Many residents work at the base, according to Rosen Rusev, the mayor, and the sound of aircraft overhead is routine.

But in late July, the Bulgarian government proposed – and Parliament approved – the deployment of as many as eight US Air Force Stratotankers and up to 250 personnel.

Within two days, residents of Bezmer and nearby villages had collected more than 3,000 signatures against the deployment and held peaceful protests.

They did not want their village to become part of the war on Iran.

Rusev said a buzzy atmosphere took hold of Bezmer on Friday, when residents realised the tankers had left.

“Now they feel their voice is finally heard,” he told Al Jazeera. “It happened just as they wanted.”

The government had moved to reassure residents. Stoyanov said military intelligence had identified no threat to national security, the US aircraft or other facilities in Bulgaria. A United Kingdom assessment requested by the government had reportedly judged the risk as extremely low.

But reassurances did little to calm everyone.

With temperatures soaring to about 30 degrees Celsius (86F), two friends, Dinka Todorova, 67, and Ganka Vlaeva, 78, sat in plastic chairs in the shade.

Both have children who work at the airbase.

“We shiver day after day and pray that the war doesn’t come here,” Vlaeva said. “We are the first target, and many people will die.”

“And children, too,” Todorova added quietly. “For the ambitions of the greedy.”

Vlaeva said she was disappointed with the government and lawmakers, accusing them of ignoring the villagers’ petition.

“They don’t want to hear the voice of the people who elected them,” she said.

Not everyone in Bezmer shared that concern.

Ivan, a 33-year-old who sat beside the village church with his electric bicycle nearby, said that “groundless panic” was spread “recklessly”.

“There’s no danger for the village,” he concluded.

He is more worried about the possibility of interceptor missiles, or “something coming from Russia across the Black Sea”.

As residents protested, Antoniya Ivanova, whose father is a serviceman at the base, hung a white sheet over an aerial photograph of Bezmer. Animated films were projected onto it for children “to wind down the accumulated stress”, she explained.

“We’re the most innocent in this whole situation,” she said. “We didn’t want those aeroplanes near our homes.”

Children filled the playground as the afternoon cooled.

“Maybe there is a chance of attacks, but I think the media exaggerates,” said Tsonka Moskova, a mother in the village. “Whatever is meant to happen will happen. Those above us decide – the government. They are to blame.”

A low-flying AS532 Cougar helicopter passed overhead. Nobody looked up. The residents are accustomed to Bulgarian military aircraft.

Rusev, the fourth-term independent mayor, spent days trying to navigate between the villagers’ fears and officials. The protests were not an attempt to bring down the government, he said.

“We just wanted adequate information about the potential threats if the planes remained stationed here and what the guarantees for our safety were,” he said.

Social media made the situation harder, he added.

In Facebook groups, officials and experts struggled to compete with thousands of comments, many speculative and panic-inducing.

Military police also patrolled the village and the area around the airbase, adding to a sense of fear for some, and a sense of safety for others.

While Bulgaria is in the range of some Iranian missiles, some analysts argue that Iran is unlikely to have the capacity – or genuine will – for successful missile attacks against Bulgaria or elsewhere in continental Europe.

On Monday, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said that the tankers had not made a single flight “south from the airport”, but had travelled to fellow NATO member nations for training and exercises.

But also on Monday, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Tehran reserved the right to counter “any action regarded as supporting US and Israeli military aggression” against it.

“We have no issue with the Bulgarian people,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said. “It was previously announced – and reports have also confirmed – that several refuelling aircraft have left Bulgarian territory.

“As many Bulgarian citizens and politicians themselves have acknowledged, this action is contrary to international law and amounts to support for the military aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime against Iran.”

Back in the village, a woman said she was not afraid of Iran’s threats.

She did not want to be named or photographed for this article.

“I am definitely not scared. God is keeping us safe,” she told Al Jazeera. “I lie down and sleep in peace, for you alone, Lord, make me live in safety,” she said, reciting a line from the Bible.

articles.title: US pauses fresh military action against Iran, turns to sanctions and maritime pressure
articles.summary: US News: The US does not intend to carry out further military strikes on Iran âfor now,â secretary of state Marco Rubio has informed the foreign ministers of s.
articles.body: The US does not intend to carry out further military strikes on Iran âfor now,â secretary of state Marco Rubio has informed the foreign ministers of several allied countries, Axios reported, citing American officials.Instead, the Trump administration plans to intensify pressure on Tehran through other measures, including Washingtonâs ongoing naval blockade of Iranian ports.âRubio conveyed Americaâs plan to avoid initiating new military strikes against Tehran âfor the time beingâ. Instead, the administration aims to intensify pressure through naval blockades and economic measures while maintaining the flow of petroleum through the vital Strait of Hormuz,â officials told Axios.However, officials stressed that the US has not ruled out military action if Tehran strikes first. They described the strategic shift as âsignificantâ, arguing that Iranâs ability to disrupt maritime energy flows through the strait has been âsubstantially reduced."According to the report, the policy could remain in place at least through the November midterm elections, after which Washington could consider resuming military action.Washington maintains that its operations near the Strait of Hormuz have âdrasticallyâ weakened one of Iranâs key tools for âmanipulatingâ global energy markets. US forces have been clearing mines from the waterway, contributing to increased tanker traffic along its southern route.The Strait of Hormuz has been under a virtual Iranian blockade since March, following US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic that triggered the wider Middle East conflict. In response, the US imposed a blockade of Iranian ports.Rubioâs reported remarks come as the US steps up its economic pressure on Iran, which the Trump administration has termed an âEconomic D-Dayâ. Washington has imposed additional sanctions and warned foreign countries doing business with Iran that they could face severe penalties.Tehran has rejected the US strategy, calling efforts to isolate its financial system unlawful. Global oil prices fell for a second consecutive day as traders appeared to factor in limited immediate disruption from the latest sanctions warnings.Amid the tensions, Iran and Oman held talks on managing maritime transit through the Strait of Hormuz. The two sides discussed establishing a temporary navigation corridor and agreed to jointly clear mines from the waterway, which has remained largely closed to normal commercial shipping.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: âShouldn't it begin with Congress?' BJP targets Rahul Gandhi over 'smash the patriarchyâ remark
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: BJP on Wednesday attacked leader of opposition in Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, over his recent âsmash the patriarchyâ remark, accusing him of h.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP on Wednesday attacked leader of opposition in Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, over his recent âsmash the patriarchyâ remark, accusing him of hypocrisy and questioning whether he applies the same principle within his own Congress party.Addressing a press conference, BJP leader and MP Bansuri Swaraj referred to Congress leaderâs August 22 remarks at an event in Pune, where he spoke about challenging patriarchal attitudes and restrictions placed on women.âOn August 22, Leader of Opposition (LoP) Rahul Gandhi tried to create a new false narrative in this country. He says, âSmash the patriarchy.â I am all for it,â Swaraj said.âBut I want to ask Rahul Gandhi ji, do you limit the slogan of âsmash the patriarchyâ only to the stage in Pune? Do you practise political patriarchy within your own Congress party?â she added.Swaraj accused Rae Bareli MP of lacking a âvisionâ and âpositive agendaâ, alleging that he uses material prepared by his research team to mislead voters and young people.BJP cites remarks against Kangana, Hema MaliniSwaraj said the Congress should begin by examining its own record if it wants to challenge patriarchy.She cited the controversy involving Congress leader Supriya Shrinate's social media account after BJP MP Kangana Ranaut was given the party ticket from Mandi during the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. Swaraj described the remarks posted from the account as âextremely objectionableâ.She also referred to comments made by Congress leader Randeep Surjewala about BJP leader and actor Hema Malini at a rally in Kaithal in April 2024.Swaraj said Surjewala was subsequently barred from campaigning for 48 hours following action over the remarks.âBut Rahul Gandhi did not âsmash the patriarchyâ then either. There was no such statement from him. Instead, he once again chose to remain silent,â she said.Swaraj also criticised Rahul over what she described as a âhighly objectionable jokeâ involving Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy, saying Gandhi had participated in it along with Congress leader Sandeep Dikshit.âIt does not befit the leader of opposition of the country to make such statements. It appears that leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi now makes statements solely for their meme and reel value,â Swaraj said.BJP MP further said, "I want to ask Rahul Gandhi, why is there not a single woman leader in Karnataka and Himachal? Why did he oppose the Women's Reservation Bill? And you are talking about women empowerment?"Highlighting Prime Minister Narendra Modi's governance model centered on women-led development, Swaraj stated, "You constantly criticize Narendra Modi, but he is a leader committed to empowering women. Currently, 48 percent of Indiaâs women are leading startups around the world. Rahul Gandhi, I am calling you out for your misogyny. This nation deserves a better Leader of the Opposition than you, Mr. Rahul Gandhi."What Rahul Gandhi said about patriarchyCongress MP's remarks came during the Congress' âChhatron Ki Goonjâ campaign in Pune, where he addressed thousands of women and girl students.He said the campaign was aimed at challenging a patriarchal system that, according to him, gives men greater freedom while imposing restrictions on women.Former Congress president referred to a video of PM Modi that he said was released after a protest at Jantar Mantar. He alleged that the Prime Minister was âculturally shockedâ when girls protesting used cuss words but had no objection to boys using similar language.âOur fight is against such a mindset. We do not want a country which gives all the freedom to men, while women continue to live in a controlled environment. We will work together to end the patriarchal system in India,â Rahul said.In an Instagram story, Congress leader had also defended actor Kriti Sanon amid criticism of her outfit in a Raksha Bandhan advertisement, saying, âWhat a woman wears, what she does and where she goes â is her choice.âHe added, âStop trolling women for exercising their freedom,â using the hashtag âsmash the patriarchyâ.The remarks followed criticism of Sanon's attire in a jewellery advertisement, including from BJP MP Kangana Ranaut.Sanon subsequently questioned why women continued to be told what to wear and said, âCulture & Traditions are in her heart, not in her neckline!âGet the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Work began in 1928 on New York Cityâs first municipal airport; today, Floyd Bennett Field spans more than 1,300 acres of grassland and marsh
articles.summary: US News: Floyd Bennett Field was intended to give New York City its own municipal airport when construction began in 1928. Today, the former airfield is part o.
articles.body: Floyd Bennett Field was intended to give New York City its own municipal airport when construction began in 1928. Today, the former airfield is part of Gateway National Recreation Area and covers more than 1,300 acres of grassland, saltmarshes, tidal mudflats and former aviation facilities. The site in southeastern Brooklyn has changed dramatically since the first airport work began. Its runways and hangars once handled commercial and record-setting flights, and it later became a major naval aviation site before the National Park Service took over the property. The history of Floyd Bennett Field is therefore a record of how one piece of New York City land moved from marshland and landfill to aviation center, military installation and urban recreation area.Construction began in 1928, but the airport opened laterNew York City began transforming the area around Barren Island in 1928, and the project involved waterways, marshes and newly placed fill, as city officials sought to establish an airport within New York's boundaries. The National Park Service's detailed history says the airport was named for naval aviator Floyd Bennett, who had been part of Commander Richard E. Byrd's 1926 flight over the North Pole. Bennett had received the Congressional Medal of Honor and died in 1928 from pneumonia that developed after injuries from an earlier plane crash.Construction took about three years, and the airport was dedicated on May 23, 1931, rather than opening as a completed municipal airport in 1928. The finished complex included concrete runways, four hangars and an administration building that served as the terminal. The site also included facilities for seaplanes, which reflected the importance of Jamaica Bay to the airport's design. A National Park Service historic district account notes that the airport was constructed between 1928 and 1931 by the city's Department of Docks. The project included two main runways, each 100 feet wide, while additional runways were added later.The airport became a center for record-setting flightsFloyd Bennett Field never became the commercial success city officials had hoped for, and New York eventually developed another municipal airport closer to the city's transportation network. That did not make the Brooklyn airfield irrelevant, since between 1931 and 1939, 26 flights that attempted to circle the world or cross the Atlantic began or ended at Floyd Bennett Field, according to the National Park Service.The field also attracted aviators attempting long-distance records. Its location and facilities gave pilots a major base for flights during the period when aviation records were drawing widespread public attention. The airport's role changed as New York expanded its aviation infrastructure. Municipal Airport No. 2, now LaGuardia Airport, opened in 1939. Floyd Bennett Field was subsequently sold to the U.S. Navy, and that transition marked the end of its first chapter as New York City's municipal airport.The Navy took over, and the airfield became a military siteOn June 2, 1941, Naval Air Station New York was dedicated at Floyd Bennett Field, and the Navy expanded the site and continued using it through and after World War II. After the war, the facility became a Naval Air Reserve Training Station in 1946. articles.title: Raids & kidnapping drills: How Chinese students are preparing for college in Trump's USA
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For most Chinese teenagers preparing to leave for American universities, the final months before departure are all about packing clothes, buying the r.
articles.body: For most Chinese teenagers preparing to leave for American universities, the final months before departure are all about packing clothes, buying the right laptop and saying goodbye to family.But some are being taught what to do if armed men burst into their rooms.According to a report by South China Morning Post, private summer camps in China are simulating encounters with US immigration authorities, including fake Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids.The message to students is stark: once they arrive in America, they must be prepared not only for academic pressure and culture shock, but also for an immigration system that has become unpredictable and hostile.The unusual training reflects a much broader shift in the way some Chinese families are thinking about American higher education.For decades, admission to a US university represented the culmination of an intensely competitive academic journey. Now, amid President Donald Trump's sweeping immigration crackdown, some parents are treating the journey as a potential security risk as well.Surviving in the USAReport of such summer camps have emerged against a backdrop of rapidly changing US immigration rules and a heightened political focus on foreign students.The Trump administration has tightened scrutiny of international students, expanded visa vetting and taken steps to make it easier for immigration authorities to act against people whose status is questioned.In 2025, the administration moved to terminate thousands of student records in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), triggering lawsuits and widespread anxiety on US campuses. The government subsequently restored access for many students whose records had been terminated, while maintaining that it had not reversed individual visa revocations.The administration also announced a tougher approach to Chinese student visas, saying it would aggressively revoke visas for some Chinese students and increase scrutiny of future applications from China and Hong Kong. Student and exchange-visitor applicants were also subjected to expanded vetting, including scrutiny of their social media presence.This has created a new calculation for Chinese families sending their children to the US.A student who has spent years preparing for university can now find that admission is only one hurdle.Getting a visa, passing security checks, maintaining legal status and avoiding behaviour that could attract immigration scrutiny have become equally important concerns.The psychological effect is significant.Students are being encouraged to understand their rights, carry documentation, think carefully about their digital footprint and know what to do if approached by immigration officers.For some families, however, the precautions have gone much further.Why Chinese parents are especially anxiousChinese students occupy a unique position in the American higher-education system.According to data cited in recent reporting, 265,919 Chinese students were enrolled at US institutions during the 2024-25 academic year. Together, Chinese and Indian students accounted for 53% of all international students in US higher education.But Chinese students also sit at the intersection of two increasingly sensitive issues: immigration and US-China national security competition.Washington has repeatedly raised concerns about technology transfer, espionage, intellectual property and China's military-civil fusion strategy. Beijing, meanwhile, has accused Washington of discriminating against Chinese students and restricting normal academic exchanges.For an ordinary teenager heading to college, the geopolitical confrontation can feel distant. But the consequences can become personal when visa decisions, social media checks or immigration enforcement enter the picture.In 2025, the number of F-1 student visas issued to Chinese applicants fell sharply. One analysis cited by US media estimated that visas issued to Chinese applicants between May and August 2025 were 46% lower than during the comparable period in 2017.That decline has reinforced fears that studying in America is becoming less predictable.China's government has itself objected to the new restrictions. After the US announced its latest student-visa changes in July 2026, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian called them discriminatory and said Beijing reserved the right to take reciprocal measures.For families who have already paid large sums for American education, the question is no longer simply whether their child can get into a US university.It is whether the child can safely and legally remain there long enough to graduate.The four-year clockThe latest change could make that anxiety even more acute.In July, the Department of Homeland Security announced a final rule ending the decades-old "duration of status" system for international students.Previously, students on F-1 visas could generally remain in the United States for the duration of their academic programme as long as they maintained their status.Under the new system, international students will generally receive a fixed period of admission of no more than four years, subject to extensions. The rule is scheduled to take effect in September.The administration says the change is designed to combat visa abuse and strengthen national-security oversight. DHS has argued that the old system allowed foreign students to remain in the country without sufficiently regular government review.Universities and immigration advocates see it differently.They point out that many doctoral, medical and research programmes routinely last longer than four years. Students could therefore face additional applications and uncertainty in the middle of their academic careers. The new rules also restrict some changes of academic programme or institution.For Chinese parents, the implication is straightforward: getting their child into an American university may no longer mean the child is secure there for the duration of the degree.There is now another deadline to worry about.And then comes the question of stayingFor many international students, the attraction of an American education has never been limited to the classroom.The possibility of gaining professional experience after graduation through Optional Practical Training, or OPT, has been an important part of the calculation.But even that pathway is now facing uncertainty.The Trump administration has considered imposing a $100,000 fee on international students seeking to work in the United States after graduation through OPT, according to a Wall Street Journal report. The proposal remains under discussion and is not established policy, but its emergence has added another layer of uncertainty for prospective students.The cumulative effect is powerful.A Chinese student planning to attend a US university may now have to think about admission, visa approval, social-media screening, immigration status, the four-year limit, possible extensions and the rules governing post-graduation employment.That is a very different proposition from the one presented to previous generations.The fear goes beyond ICEPerhaps the most striking aspect of the reported training camps is that some of the exercises are not even directly about immigration law.The kidnapping drills point to a deeper anxiety: the belief among some parents that their children will be entering an unfamiliar country where they may be vulnerable and far from home.This fear is amplified by China's enormous distance from the US and by the fact that many students leaving for American colleges are teenagers or young adults experiencing independent life abroad for the first time.The drills therefore combine several anxieties into one: immigration enforcement, crime, political instability, unfamiliar laws and the fear that a young student may not know how to respond in a crisis.It is important, however, not to confuse these fears with evidence that Chinese students routinely face kidnapping or that ICE is conducting indiscriminate raids on foreign students.There is no evidence that such dangers are a normal part of student life in the United States.What the drills reveal is something different: how the perception of risk has changed.Parents do not necessarily need to believe that a kidnapping will happen to decide that their child should know what to do if it does.Likewise, a student does not need to expect an ICE encounter to feel anxious about what would happen if immigration officers questioned their status.The social media problemThe atmosphere surrounding visa screening has also changed how international students behave online.In 2025, international students told the Washington Post that they were deleting posts, unfollowing political accounts and scrutinising years of social-media activity because they feared that jokes, memes, political opinions or other online activity could jeopardise their visa applications.The State Department's expanded vetting policy has made digital behaviour an increasingly important part of the immigration process.For Chinese students, that creates a particularly sensitive environment because virtually every aspect of US-China relations can become politically charged.A student can be academically exceptional and have no connection to politics or national security issues, yet still worry that something posted years earlier could be misunderstood.That produces a form of self-censorship that begins before the student ever boards an aircraft.A new generation arrives in America differentlyThe result is a striking transformation in the psychology of studying abroad.Previous generations of Chinese students often arrived in America with one overriding objective: succeed academically.Today's students may arrive with a second mission: avoid becoming entangled in America's increasingly aggressive immigration and national security machinery.That does not mean Chinese students are abandoning the United States.American universities remain enormously attractive because of their academic reputation, research opportunities and global career networks.But the decision is becoming more complicated.For parents paying tens of thousands of dollars in tuition and sending their children thousands of kilometres away, uncertainty carries a price of its own.The kidnapping drills may therefore be less about preparing students for a specific threat than about preparing them for a world in which the rules appear to be changing faster than families can keep up.The irony is hard to miss.America's universities have long marketed themselves as places where young people from around the world can come to learn, experiment and build their futures.Now, some Chinese teenagers are arriving at those same campuses after being taught what to do if someone breaks into their room, takes their phone or threatens to deport them.That is the real significance of the drills.They are not evidence that America has suddenly become a war zone for Chinese students.They are evidence that the psychological border between immigration enforcement and everyday student life has become much thinner.And as Trump's immigration policies continue to tighten the rules around who can enter, how long they can stay and what they can do after graduation, some Chinese families are responding in the most dramatic way possible: by training their children not just to study in America, but to survive the uncertainty of studying there.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: At least eight killed, hundreds missing after Nepal flash flood
articles.summary: Across the border, Tibet reported “major casualties” with people missing in the neighbouring county of Gyirong.
articles.body:
Nepal sent helicopters to the rescue after a huge flash ⁠flood swept away villages, killing at least eight people and damaging roads, bridges and power projects in areas near Tibet, authorities said.

Officials said 384 tourists, including 291 from countries including the United Kingdom, the United States, India and Malaysia were reported missing as a result of the flash flood on Wednesday.

list 1 of 4 What caused Nepal’s devastating flood damage and how was it contained?

list 2 of 4 After the floods of 2025, can we keep 2026 above water?

list 3 of 4 Landslide hits bus in northern India, killing 15, as rescue continues

list 4 of 4 Rescuers search for survivors amid risk of fresh floods in Afghanistan

The waters were too high for helicopters to land in Nepal’s affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa, with a population of about 50,000, officials said.

“There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” district administrator Narendra ‌Pariyar told the Reuters news agency. “But I cannot say for sure now.”

Pariyar urged those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi River in the area to seek higher ground, pointing to reports that nearby villages and infrastructure project sites were washed away.

Across the border, Tibet reported “major casualties” with people missing in the neighbouring county of Gyirong after a mudslide ⁠hit a land crossing between China and Nepal, the Xinhua official news agency said.

The mudslide hit China’s Gyirong port, cutting off roads, communications and power in the Shigatse region, Xinhua added, without giving details.

President Xi Jinping urged “all-out” efforts to search ⁠for the missing, and ⁠called for strengthening monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.

Prayash Adhikari, a climate justice activist in Nepal, said that the “devastating” flood has wiped out “whole villages”.

“Hundreds of people are missing,” Adhikari told Al Jazeera from Kathamandu, stating that it wiped out buildings, schools, bridges and highways.

Videos shared by Nepal Police and others on social media showed torrents of muddy water crashing through mountain valleys.

Many people were caught off guard when the flash flood hit, as there was no heavy rainfall, said Kosh Raj Koirala Kway-rarla, an editor of Republica Daily, an English newspaper in Nepal’s capital.

“[People] were at home … several houses have been washed away, swept away by the river,” Kway-rarla told Al Jazeera.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah convened an emergency meeting of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority to take stock of the situation.

“Work has started to take necessary steps in coordination with the medical team, scouts, and Red Cross,” Shah said in a social media post.

The Nepal Army said it had deployed helicopters and disaster response personnel to the affected area.

“The work of collecting details of the damage is under way,” it said in a statement.

The Nepal Electricity Authority said about 430 megawatts of production capacity, including from hydropower and solar facilities, have been damaged.

“The disaster has damaged the production, transmission and distribution facilities of the Authority … resulting in disruption of electricity supply,” it said.

Several highways were also closed, authorities said.

‘Glacial lake outburst’ could be underlying cause

Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused the flash flood.

The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi River, witnessed maximum flooding on Wednesday, they said.

“The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group.

Adhikari told Al Jazeera that early warning systems are crucial to protect communities, said Adhikari.

“This can’t be completely turned around because we are on the verge of climate catastrophe, but still we can protect our communities,” he said.

The ⁠Bhote Koshi River originates in Tibet ⁠and empties into Nepal’s Trishuli River that eventually flows into India as the Gandak River.

A flood last year in the Bhote Koshi River killed nine people, ‌with 24 missing, and washed away the “Friendship Bridge” linking Nepal and China, disrupting transport and trade for several months. That flood ‌was ‌triggered by the draining of a supraglacial lake in Tibet, a regional climate monitor said.

Monsoon rains from June to September regularly trigger deadly floods and landslides across South Asia.

Scientists say climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in the region.

A flood last year in the Bhote Koshi River killed nine people, ‌with 24 missing, and washed away the “Friendship Bridge” linking Nepal and China, disrupting transport and trade for several months. That flood ‌was ‌triggered by the draining of a supraglacial lake in Tibet, a regional climate monitor said.
Monsoon rains from June to September regularly trigger deadly floods and landslides across South Asia.
Scientists say climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in the region.

articles.title: Sheffield delivery robots removed from streets as pilot ends
articles.summary: Operator Starship Technologies says the end of the trial is not due to vandalism of the machines.
articles.body:
Self-driving food delivery robots have been taken off the streets after the operator called time on a pilot scheme after just five months.

The six-wheeled machines were launched in parts of Sheffield by Starship Technologies in March in partnership with Uber Eats.

During the short trial the foot-high vehicles kept getting their visibility flags snapped off and some were sprayed with graffiti, as well as attracting complaints that they "got in the way" of pedestrians.

Starship Technologies said it had "paused" the service as its pilot scheme had come to a "natural" end, but insisted the vandalism did not affect the decision to stop.

Delivery robots tasked with carrying supermarket and takeaway orders have become a familiar sight in major UK cities, including Leeds and London.

They have divided opinion, with some people praising their nimbleness and convenience, while critics have complained they obstruct pavements and carry a "sinister" number of cameras.

But while they have become a permanent feature in parts of Leeds, Starship said the service had been halted in Sheffield for now.

As well as the robots themselves falling victim to vandalism in March, a charging station was defaced and traffic cones were placed behind the robots to prevent them from moving .

Ryan Case, public affairs and communication manager at Starship said: "Our pilot in Sheffield has come to an end, and we have paused the service while we review what we've learned.

"There have been a small number of incidents of vandalism, which is disappointing, not least because it affects the local businesses that rely on the robots for deliveries.

"But vandalism wasn't a factor in our decision to pause the service: this was a commercial decision and a natural conclusion to the pilot phase."

articles.title: HELOC and home equity loan rates today, Wednesday, August 26, 2026: Why locking in a low rate matters
articles.summary: These are the HELOC and home equity loan rates for Wednesday, August 26, 2026. The average HELOC adjustable rate is 7.16%, a new 2026 low. The national avera...
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Interest rates vary between lenders, so comparison shopping home equity loan and line of credit lenders can save you thousands over the life of your loan. For home equity loans, securing the lowest fixed rate matters since you'll be stuck with it for the life of the loan. For HELOCs, locking in the lowest possible introductory rate is key, since your interest rate is likely to fluctuate, even rise, over the loan term.

HELOC and home equity loan rates: Wednesday, August 26, 2026

The average HELOC adjustable rate is 7.16% , a new 2026 low, according to real estate data analytics company Curinos.

The national average rate on a fixed-rate home equity loan is 7.35% , up slightly from its 2026 low of 7.31% in late June.

Both rates are based on applicants with a minimum credit score of 780 and a maximum combined loan-to-value ratio (CLTV) of less than 70%.

Most HELOCs are variable-rate products, meaning their interest rates are tied to an external interest rate. When that rate rises or falls, the rate on your HELOC generally follows suit.

HELOCs are typically tied to the prime rate , the baseline rate banks currently charge their most creditworthy customers.

The best HELOC lenders will assess the risk any borrower presents and add a margin to protect themselves. Riskier borrowers will have larger margins, while those considered less risky will receive smaller ones. Factors such as your credit score, debt-to-income ratio (DTI), and loan-to-value ratio (LTV) will all be considered in this assessment.

How do home equity loan interest rates work?

A home equity loan and its interest rate work like a HELOC in some ways and like a traditional primary mortgage in others.

As with a HELOC, the prime rate usually impacts your home equity loan rates, and home equity loan lenders incorporate a margin into your rate. Both HELOC and home equity loan rates are loosely influenced by the Federal Reserve's federal funds rate and broader economic conditions.

However, like many first mortgages, home equity loans are typically fixed-rate products, meaning you'll have the same interest rate for the entire term. Fixed-rate HELOCs exist, but they're much less common.

Learn more: HELOC and home equity loan interest rates: How they work and what you can expect to pay

How to qualify for a HELOC or home equity loan

Specific loan requirements vary by lender, but generally, home equity loans and HELOCs require a borrower to:

Have a FICO credit score of 680 or higher

Show a history of good credit and proof of sufficient monthly income

Obtain an appraisal to determine the current market value of the home

Have at least 15% to 20% equity in the house

Have a debt-to-income ratio of 43% or less

Show proof of in-force homeowners insurance

Lenders may charge origination fees and other closing costs on a HELOC or home equity loan. When shopping for yours, make sure to ask about all possible application fees, annual charges, early account closure fees, and other one-time or ongoing expenses. Shop multiple lenders to find the lowest interest rate and the fewest fees.

What is a good interest rate on a HELOC or a HEL right now?

Rates vary significantly from one lender to the next. You may see rates from nearly 6% to as much as 18%. It really depends on your creditworthiness and how diligent you are as a shopper. The national average for a HELOC is 7.16% , and 7.35% for a home equity loan. Those can serve as a guide when shopping rates from second mortgage lenders.

Is it a good idea to get a HELOC or a home equity loan right now?

For homeowners with low primary mortgage rates and significant equity in their homes, it's likely a good idea to consider a HELOC or a home equity loan now. First off, rates are the lowest in years. And you don't give up that great primary mortgage rate that you earned when you bought your house. You can use cash drawn from your equity for home improvements , repairs, and upgrades. Or virtually anything else.

What is the monthly payment on a $50,000 home equity line of credit?

If you withdraw the full $50,000 from a home equity line of credit and pay a 7.25% interest rate, for example, your monthly payment during the 10-year HELOC draw period would be about $302. That sounds good, but remember that the rate is usually variable, so it changes periodically, and your payments will increase during the 20-year repayment period. A HELOC essentially becomes a 30-year loan. HELOCs and HELs are best if you borrow and repay the balance within a much shorter period.

How do fixed-rate HELOCs work, and which lenders offer them?

Home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) usually charge variable rates, but you can find fixed-rate HELOCs with certain lenders. Learn how a fixed-rate HELOC works.

It can be a good time to get a HELOC, especially if you don't want to lose the low rate on your first mortgage. Learn how the housing market could affect your decision.

The best HELOC lenders have flexible payment options, allow high CLTV ratios, and more. Read through our top picks to find the best HELOC lender for you.

Is a HELOC a good idea? Pros and cons to consider.

A home equity line of credit (HELOC) can help many homeowners, but it’s not right for everyone. Before you take one out, consider the pros and cons.

HELOCs have changed — and some homeowners may not like the new rules

HELOCs are changing as nonbank lenders reshape the market. Learn how minimum draw requirements affect borrowers and how to find a flexible HELOC.

The amount you can borrow with a HELOC depends on your home value, outstanding mortgage balance, and lender. Learn to calculate how much HELOC money you can get.

articles.summary: On Wednesday, August 26, 2026, some of the highest CD rates are at 4% APY or more. Not sure where to find them? Learn more about where to get the best CD rat...
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Deposit account rates are on the decline. The good news: You can lock in a competitive return on a certificate of deposit (CD) today and preserve your earning power. In fact, the best CDs still pay rates of 4% or higher. Read on for a snapshot of CD rates today and where to find the best offers.

CDs today typically offer rates significantly higher than traditional savings accounts. Currently, the best short-term CDs (six to 12 months) generally offer rates around 4% to 4.5% APY.

Today, Wednesday, August 26, 2026 , the highest CD rate is 4.30% . Synchrony Bank offers this rate on its 16-month CD, and Marcus by Goldman Sachs offers it on its 18-month CD.

The following is a look at some of the best CD rates available today from our verified partners:

The 2000s were marked by the dot-com bubble and later, the global financial crisis of 2008. Though the early 2000s saw relatively higher CD rates, they began to fall as the economy slowed and the Federal Reserve cut its target rate to stimulate growth. By 2009, in the aftermath of the financial crisis, the average one-year CD paid around 1% APY, with five-year CDs at less than 2% APY.

The trend of falling CD rates continued into the 2010s, especially after the Great Recession of 2007-2009. The Fed's policies to stimulate the economy (in particular, its decision to keep its benchmark interest rate near zero) led banks to offer very low rates on CDs. By 2013, average rates on 6-month CDs fell to about 0.1% APY, while 5-year CDs returned an average of 0.8% APY.

However, things changed between 2015 and 2018, when the Fed started gradually increasing rates again. At this point, CD rates showed a slight improvement as the economy expanded, marking the end of nearly a decade of ultra-low rates. However, the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020 led to emergency rate cuts by the Fed, causing CD rates to fall to new record lows.

The situation reversed following the pandemic as inflation began to spiral out of control. This prompted the Fed to hike rates 11 times between March 2022 and July 2023. In turn, this led to higher rates on loans and higher APYs on savings products, including CDs.

Fast forward to September 2024 — the Fed finally decided to start cutting the federal funds rate after it determined that inflation was essentially under control. In 2025, it announced three additional rate cuts. Today, we're seeing CD rates steadily declining from their peak. Even so, CD rates remain high by historical standards.

Take a look at how CD rates have changed since 2009:

Traditionally, longer-term CDs have offered higher interest rates compared to shorter-term CDs. This is because locking in money for a longer period typically carries more risk (namely, missing out on higher future rates), which banks compensate for with higher rates.

However, this pattern doesn't necessarily hold today; the highest average CD rate is for a 12-month term. This indicates a flattening or inversion of the yield curve, which can happen in uncertain economic times or when investors expect future interest rates to decline.

When opening a CD , choosing one with a high APY is just one piece of the puzzle. There are other factors that can impact whether a particular CD is best for your needs and your overall return. Consider the following when choosing a CD:

Your goals: Decide how long you're willing to lock away your funds. CDs have fixed terms, and withdrawing your money before the term ends can incur penalties. Common terms range from a few months up to several years. The right term for you depends on when you anticipate needing access to your money.

Type of financial institution: Rates can vary significantly among financial institutions. Don't just check with your current bank; research CD rates from online banks, local banks, and credit unions. Online banks , in particular, often offer higher interest rates than traditional brick-and-mortar banks because they have lower overhead costs. However, make sure any online bank you consider is FDIC-insured (or NCUA-insured for credit unions).

Account terms: Beyond the interest rate, understand the terms of the CD, including the maturity date and withdrawal penalties . Also, check whether there's a minimum deposit requirement and, if so, whether it fits your budget.

Inflation: While CDs can offer safe, fixed returns, they may not keep pace with inflation , especially over longer terms. Consider this when deciding on the term and amount to invest.

Is a certificate of deposit (CD) still a good investment?

Is a certificate of deposit a good investment right now? That depends on your timeline and goals. Learn more about whether now is a good time to invest in CDs.

articles.title: Missouri grandma ordered to stop serving free breakfasts refuses to back down, 'They are my family'
articles.summary: Kathy Kite says she won't stop serving free breakfast in Harrisburg, Missouri, despite a health department letter saying she needs a permit
articles.body: A Missouri grandmother says she was frightened she could end up in legal trouble after county health officials told her to stop serving free homemade breakfasts without a permit, but she told Fox News Digital she has no intention of giving up the morning tradition that brings her tiny community together. "I'm not gonna stop providing for my community," Kathy Kite of Harrisburg, Missouri, told Fox News Digital in an interview Tuesday. "I wouldn't stop feeding my children, I wouldn't stop feeding my family. I'm not gonna stop feeding my community cause they are my family….This is bigger than that. It's about love and appreciation because they appreciate what I do." Kite has been cooking a free breakfasts for her neighbors and friends since May. In July, she received a letter from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department that said she needed to obtain a food permit or face possible legal action. YOU SHOULDN’T NEED A PERMIT TO PRAY IN YOUR OWN HOME — THE SUPREME COURT SHOULD AGREE "I got the letter in July, it upset me, because I didn't understand what I was doing wrong," Kite said. "It hurt my feelings, and it upset me because I knew at that point I was afraid I was gonna go to jail because the letter stated that if I didn't stop making breakfast for my community, that I was facing fines and jail, and so I posted it on Facebook and people responded."  The Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department denied that their letter threatened jail time, in comments to Fox News Digital. Kite said that after the local gas station where she works stopped serving breakfast following COVID, regular customers kept asking for it, so she invited them to her home and began cooking breakfast for them, herself. Kite said that what began as an early-morning breakfast for a few regulars quickly spread across the town of fewer than 300 people. More residents began stopping by for coffee and breakfast, staying to talk about farming, the weather and childhood memories. The growing sense of community motivated her to wake up even earlier to cook, and soon local mothers were bringing their children by for breakfast before school. ORTHODOX JEW ASKS SUPREME COURT TO HEAR CASE AFTER CITY ALLEGEDLY TARGETED HIS HOME PRAYER GROUP Kite said the letter from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department says that she must install a commercial kitchen in her home. "In order for me to comply with what they're asking, I would have to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to have a commercial kitchen in my home," Kite said. "I live in a 115-year-old home. It's a beautiful home. I'm not gonna jeopardize the integrity of my home to put a commercial kitchen in to make some free burritos." She said she would welcome city officials into her home so they could see firsthand what she is doing. "Come have a burrito. I'm [not] doing anything wrong. I don't, I just, I can't understand. Come to my home, see my home, and see that my home is not dirty," Kite said. "I don't have cats. I'm not making people sick. I am just a grandma cooking a meal for my friends and family and enjoying life." The Goldwater Institute sent a letter Thursday to the Boone County health department demanding they answer questions by Friday about their legal reasoning. The group said that no lawsuit has been filed to date, but it is on the table. GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS In a statement to Fox News Digital, Dave Roland, Goldwater Institute's director of allied litigation, said, "Kathy’s story is a textbook example of bureaucracy run amok. Citizens should not be required to get the government’s permission before offering passers-by some coffee and a bite to eat while they socialize. The government exists to protect this sort of neighborly kindness, not to punish it." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department told Fox News Digital that food permits are not required when providing food for family and friends, but a permit is required when providing food to the public, citing the Missouri food code. "At the time the complaint was received, Ms. Kite’s home had an open sign, tip jar, advertised food on social media and a sign in her yard — all things that are typically associated with a food establishment," the spokesperson said. "No citations or cease-and-desist orders were issued," the statement continued. "We also did not threaten jail time. We sent a letter to Ms. Kite following a complaint we received that food served in her establishment made someone ill. Our role in public health is to work with food establishments to promote safe food practices and prevent food-borne illnesses. There are safe, allowable ways to provide homemade food to the community with and without a food permit. We regularly work together with individuals and businesses who want to provide free food to the community."

articles.title: Aroundtown Q2 Earnings Call Highlights
articles.summary: Aroundtown (ETR:AT1) reported stable first-half operating results for 2026, with rental growth offsetting the impact of asset sales, while higher financing c...
articles.body:
Aroundtown (ETR:AT1) reported stable first-half operating results for 2026, with rental growth offsetting the impact of asset sales, while higher financing costs reduced funds from operations. Management said the company remains on track to meet its full-year guidance and is continuing to recycle capital through disposals, property investments and share repurchases.

CEO Barak Bar-Hen said the macroeconomic and geopolitical backdrop remained mixed during the first half, but external volatility had not materially affected operations. He said the company's residential and hotel holdings, which together represent 53% of the portfolio, continued to benefit from favorable market conditions, while the office segment remained relatively stable despite subdued economic activity.

→ Rocket Lab's Sell-Off Is Fading—Is It Finally Safe to Buy?

Net rental income totaled €591 million in the first half, unchanged from the prior-year period. Like-for-like rental growth of 2.7% offset the reduction in rental income from net disposals. Adjusted EBITDA was also broadly stable at €500 million, compared with €501 million a year earlier.

FFO I, a key recurring earnings measure for property companies, declined 4% to €144 million from €150 million, primarily due to higher financing expenses. FFO I per share was €0.13, compared with €0.14 in the first half of 2025, with the share buyback supporting the per-share outcome.

→ Travel + Leisure Goes Big—Is It Ready to Rally?

Finance expenses rose to €142 million, reflecting refinancing measures completed during 2025 and the first half of 2026. CFO Jonas Tintelnot said the company's cost of debt stood at 2.4% as of June 30 and increased to 2.6% on a post-reporting-date basis following additional refinancing activity.

Overall profit for the period was €218 million, down from €578 million in the first half of 2025. The company said its full portfolio underwent external valuation during the reporting period, resulting in valuations that were stable compared with December 2025. EPRA NTA increased 3% to €8.00 per share, while EPRA NRV rose 2% to €9.60 per share.

Portfolio growth led by residential and hotels

→ What Rising Delivery Forecasts Say About Rivian's Stock Prospects

Aroundtown's portfolio was valued at €25.2 billion as of June, with annualized rental income of €1.16 billion. Residential assets represented 33% of portfolio value, offices 34%, hotels 20%, development and investment property 7%, and logistics and retail 6%.

articles.title: Indian-origin Toronto man found dead at home; homicide angle being probed
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Toronto Police identify Indian-origin man Satwant 'Sonny' Sangha, 41, as a homicide victim following his mysterious death. Ongoing investigation raises concerns after recent violent incidents in the community.
articles.body: An Indian-origin man found dead at a Toronto home last week has been identified as a homicide victim, police said.Satwant âSonnyâ Sangha, 41, of Toronto, was found deceased at a residence near McGill Street and Church Street in downtown Toronto, according to the Toronto Police.Officers were called to the property at around 1:43 am on Friday, August 21, after receiving a report of a sudden death. Police attended the residence and found Sangha dead.An autopsy was later conducted and found signs of trauma on his body, leading investigators to classify the death as a homicide.Sangha's death is the 23rd homicide recorded in Toronto in 2026, as per the report.Authorities have not released further details about the nature of the injuries and how Sangha died. Police have also not announced any arrests or identified a suspect in connection with the case.Last month, another Indian-origin woman, 26-year-old Navneet Kaur, was fatally shot in a targeted attack in Toronto. Police later arrested a 37-year-old Brampton man and charged him with first-degree murder.The investigation is underway.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Iranian assassination plot against Netanyahu's son Yair foiled in Florida: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's eldest son, Yair Netanyahu, was the target of an alleged Iranian assassination plot while he was living in.
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's eldest son, Yair Netanyahu, was the target of an alleged Iranian assassination plot while he was living in South Florida, according to a Newsmax report.The report cited a US law-enforcement source familiar with the matter, and is an added development to Netanyahu's disclosure that Iran had tried to kill one of his sons.Netanyahu said Monday that Iran had targeted one of his two sons but did not identify him at the time. "Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to murder him, tried to murder one of my sons," Netanyahu said during a phone interview with Israel's Channel 14.According to the Newsmax report, the target was 35-year-old Yair, who had been living in the Miami area. The report said Israeli intelligence learned in December 2025 of an alleged Iranian plot against him and alerted US authorities.A US law-enforcement source cited by Newsmax said Israeli intelligence believed Iranian operatives were already in the Miami area and had conducted surveillance of Yair's residence and movements. Yair, who travels with an Israeli security detail, was then instructed to leave Florida immediately, according to the report.He reportedly returned to Israel without taking his belongings and has remained there since. The Times of Israel separately reported the Newsmax account on Wednesday.The report helps explain Netanyahu's comments about the security provided to his family. In his Channel 14 interview, he defended the need for protection for his wife, Sara, and sons Yair and Avner, saying such security was necessary because threats against his family could otherwise succeed.Wider Iranian targetingThe alleged plot against Yair comes as Iranian threats against senior Israeli and US figures and their families have intensified. Netanyahu's comments came shortly after Iranian state television aired a video targeting US President Donald Trump's 20-year-old son, Barron Trump.The roughly three-minute broadcast, aired by Iranian state television and circulated by media linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, discussed a potential plot to kill Barron and claimed that his movements were being monitored. It also alleged that a $10 million bounty had been offered for his killing, although that claim has not been independently verified.The US Secret Service said Tuesday that it was aware of the video and was investigating it as a potential threat to a protected person.The Barron video followed an earlier Iran-linked video targeting first lady Melania Trump and comes against the backdrop of longstanding Iranian threats against Trump himself.US authorities have previously accused members or alleged assets of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of pursuing assassination plots against American officials, including former national security adviser John Bolton.The reported targeting of Yair also comes as Israel has extended security arrangements for Netanyahu's immediate family. In July, Israel's Ministerial Committee for Shin Bet Affairs approved extended personal protection for Sara Netanyahu and both sons, Yair and Avner.Netanyahu has also asked Shin Bet chief David Zini to ensure appropriate protection for prime ministerial candidates, framing the issue as particularly sensitive during Israel's election campaign.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Questions don't stop with batons': Rahul Gandhi attacks Bihar govt over BPSC protests
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday waded into Biharâs escalating BPSC row, questioning the Samrat Choudhary-led gover.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi on Wednesday waded into Biharâs escalating BPSC row, questioning the Samrat Choudhary-led government over allegations of exam irregularities and paper leaks. He referred to the police crackdown on protesting students, saying, âquestions don't stop with batons.âHis statement came a day after a clash broke out between students and police in Bihar's capital, with police using water cannons and barricades to stop the protesters from marching.Rahul described it as a âstraightforwardâ question on behalf of Biharâs students and posted on X: âWhy the irregularities in recruitment exams? Why no action on allegations of paper leaks? And how long will this tampering with the future of the youth continue?âHe then targeted the long-standing BJP-JD(U)-led government in Bihar, saying, âThe controversy over BPSC exams is not of today. Students have been on the streets for a long time over the recruitment process, exam pattern, delays, and transparency.âThe Lok Sabha leader of opposition also referred to the use of an AK-47 by a security personnel during an earlier student protest in Bihar, which coincided with student protests in Delhi and across the country over NEET fiasco.âBut instead of answering, what is the government doing? It's wielding batons and water cannons. It's taking students into custody. In Siwan, there was even firing with an AK 47 on protesters,â the former Congress chief said.He added in his post: âThis is not just a question of police action. This is a question of the mindset of that BJP government, which has no answers - and that's why it's turning the police into a weapon to evade accountability.ââThe BJP government should understand this - questions don't stop with batons. You can't snatch away someone's future by instilling fear,â the Rae Bareli added.Bihar students had marched towards Raj Bhavan and chief minister Samrat Choudhary's residence to stage a âgheraoâ, but faced police barricading and some of them were detained in Patna.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Les Paulâs 7-acre New Jersey home, studio and workshop sold for $990,000 in July; weeks later the property where he pioneered multitrack recording was demolished, and his son says the family got no warning
articles.summary: US News: The New Jersey home where legendary guitarist and inventor Les Paul lived, worked and helped reshape modern music recording has been demolished, just .
articles.body: The New Jersey home where legendary guitarist and inventor Les Paul lived, worked and helped reshape modern music recording has been demolished, just weeks after the seven-acre Mahwah property was sold for $990,000. The loss drew particular attention because the house was not simply a former celebrity residence; it included the spaces where Paul experimented with sound, developed recording techniques and worked on ideas that would influence generations of musicians and producers. Les Paulâs son, Gene Paul, spoke about the demolition in a Facebook post, saying the family received no advance warning that the property was going to be demolished. He described the loss of the home as deeply painful and questioned how the property had been handled.What was lost with the Mahwah home?The property was sold on July 22, 2026, for $990,000, according to reporting by Stephanie Iken. It was a more than 6,300-square-foot home on seven acres in Mahwah's Deerhaven community. Within weeks, the structure had been demolished. The controversy stems from what the building represented. According to Guitar Player, Les Paul used the Mahwah property as a home, workshop and laboratory, where he developed pioneering multitrack recording techniques, experimented with electric-guitar technology and worked on pickup designs. He and Mary Ford also recorded songs and their television show at the house.For Gene Paul, therefore, the demolition was about more than the disappearance of an old house. In his Facebook post, he described the property as his father's workshop and laboratory and said its destruction was deeply upsetting. He questioned how the property had been handled and why his family had not been given a meaningful opportunity to be involved.His son says the family had no warningIn his Facebook post, Gene Paul said his family was given no advance warning of the demolition and was not given an opportunity to enter the house before it was destroyed. He described seeing his father's former home gutted and questioned why the family had not been consulted about its fate. The loss also raised concerns about what remained inside. A statement from the Les Paul Legacy Group, cited by Guitar Player, said that people close to Paul made a last-minute effort to save historically significant material, including handwritten research notes and Paul's workbenches. According to the group, some of those items were found in rooms that had suffered water damage and mold after years of alleged neglect by the foundation.Those claims have added another layer to the dispute, shifting the conversation beyond the demolition itself to questions about preservation, ownership and responsibility for protecting historically significant spaces.Why the property mattered to music historyLes Paul was far more than a celebrated guitarist. His experiments with sound and recording helped lay the foundations for techniques that later became central to modern music production. At the Mahwah property, his work included pioneering experiments with multitrack recording and electric-guitar technology. The site also became a destination for prominent musicians; famous guitarists visited Paul there to discuss music and technology.That history is why Gene Paul and others have objected to describing the property as simply an old building. Its significance, they argue, lay not only in its association with a famous musician but also in the work that took place within it. The home was also closely connected to Les Paul and Mary Ford's musical and television careers.
